title: One soul at the root of every family tree.
subtitle: Why kinship is named right beside Allah

row.title: Allah
sub: by whom you ask each other

then: The surah opens in Madinah after Uhud, when many families had lost fathers and sons. People would say, I ask you by Allah, and by the tie between us. The verse takes both seriously: {idea}guard your duty to Allah and do not cut the ties of the womb.{/idea} Once, when poor visitors arrived in worn wool, the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and urged people to give.
now: The cousin you have not called since the funeral. The aunt muted in the family group chat. The sibling you only see at weddings. {trap}A tie can fade without one loud fight.{/trap} The verse reminds you that every one of them comes from the same two people as you, {idea}and Allah is watching how you hold the thread.{/idea}
old: Family is complicated, so a little distance is fine.
new: Keeping family ties is part of how I stand before Allah, who watches all of it.
try: Send one warm message today to a relative you have drifted from. No agenda.

title: A sheep for a sheep is not always fair.
subtitle: The quiet swap that cheats someone who cannot check

row.title: a great sin
sub: taking from someone who cannot object

then: After Uhud, many children in Madinah were left without fathers, and their wealth sat with guardians. Some guardians would take a fat sheep and leave a thin one, saying {trap}a sheep for a sheep{/trap}, or swap a good coin for a fake. The verse names this plainly: {idea}hand their wealth over whole, and do not blend it into yours.{/idea}
now: You manage the shared account for an elderly parent. You hold your younger brother's savings. You are the one with the password. {trap}Small swaps feel invisible when the other person cannot check.{/trap} {idea}Being trusted is the exact moment to be most careful.{/idea}
old: If the numbers roughly balance, nobody is hurt.
new: When someone cannot watch over their own share, I owe it extra care, not less.
try: Look at one thing you hold for someone else. Make sure it is clearly theirs and untouched.

title: The fear of being unjust is meant to stop you.
subtitle: Honest self-doubt as a guard against harm

key.label: The test the verse keeps returning to

row.title: can I be just?
sub: if you fear not, hold back

then: A'ishah explained that this verse was about an orphan girl living with her guardian. {trap}Her wealth and beauty could tempt him to marry her without giving her what was rightfully hers.{/trap} The verse kept asking one question again and again: {idea}do you fear you will not be fair?{/idea} The details of the ruling belong to the scholars.
now: You are about to take on something that puts another person's wellbeing in your hands. A promotion over a team. A new commitment. You already sense you might not manage it fairly. {idea}That small fear is not weakness. It is a warning light.{/idea}
old: If something is allowed, I can take it on and work out fairness later.
new: If I honestly fear I will be unfair, that fear is a reason to choose the lighter path.
try: Before your next big yes, ask yourself one question: can I be fair to everyone this touches?

title: A gift given with a good heart.
subtitle: What she is given is hers, freely
then: In the society the surah was reforming, women's rights in marriage were often brushed aside, as the verse before showed with orphan girls. This verse sets the tone: {idea}the bridal gift is hers, given gladly.{/idea} Anything she gives back must come {reward}from her own good pleasure{/reward}, not pressure.
now: Think about how gifts work in your home. The money a spouse earned, the thing a parent gave a child, the present that later gets "borrowed" back. {trap}A gift taken back by pressure was never really a gift.{/trap} {idea}Generosity that is freely given and freely returned keeps hearts at ease.{/idea}
old: Once it is in the family, it does not matter whose it is.
new: What I give should be given gladly, and what comes back should come back freely.
try: Give someone at home a small gift today, and expect nothing for it.

title: Wealth is a support, so handle it with care.
subtitle: Provide, clothe, and speak kindly
then: The surah was building a new community in Madinah, with families caring for orphans and dependents after Uhud. The verse calls wealth {reward}a means of support{/reward} that Allah gave, not a toy to hand over carelessly. And it adds something easy to miss: {idea}speak to those in your care with kindness.{/idea}
now: You pay for everything at home, and you are tired. The kids ask for more, and your answer comes out sharp. {trap}Paying the bills can start to feel like it is enough.{/trap} The verse puts the kind word right next to the food and clothes. {idea}Both are part of providing.{/idea}
old: As long as I pay for things, how I talk about it does not matter.
new: Providing well includes the words I use with the people I provide for.
try: Next time someone at home asks you for something, answer gently, even if the answer is no.

title: Hand it back whole, with witnesses, and Allah as Reckoner.
subtitle: The guardian's job ends in an honest handover
then: Guardians in Madinah held the wealth of children whose fathers had died. The verse names a quiet temptation: {trap}using it up quickly before the child grows up and asks for it.{/trap} The handover is to be clear and witnessed, and {idea}Allah is enough as the One who takes account.{/idea}
now: You managed your younger sibling's money while they studied. Or you handled a parent's affairs for years. Now they want it back. {trap}It is tempting to blur the numbers or explain away the gaps.{/trap} {reward}A clean handover, in the open, frees you too.{/reward}
old: I looked after it, so some of it is mine to use however I like.
new: A trust ends well only when I can hand it back openly, knowing Allah saw every step.
try: If you hold anything for someone, write down what it is and where it stands today.

title: Women and children were left out. Not anymore.
subtitle: A share for those who used to get nothing
then: Before Islam, it was common for {trap}grown men to take the inheritance while women and children got nothing.{/trap} A woman named Umm Kujjah came to the Prophet ﷺ worried for her two daughters, left with nothing after their father died. The verse answered: {idea}women have a share too, whether the estate is little or much.{/idea} The detailed shares come in the verses that follow.
now: The family meeting after a death. Someone says she does not need much, he has kids, she is married, let us keep it simple. {trap}The quiet person in the room often gets overlooked.{/trap} {idea}Allah named their share before anyone could vote them out of it.{/idea}
old: Some people in the family obviously matter more when it comes to money.
new: Allah gave a place to those people tend to overlook, so I should not overlook them either.
try: Think of the quietest person in your family. Ask how they are doing, and really listen.

title: Those watching from the doorway deserve something too.
subtitle: Kindness to the ones with no share
then: When an estate was being divided, poor relatives, orphans, and the needy would sometimes be present. Ibn Abbas described how {trap}their hearts would long for something as they watched each heir take a share.{/trap} The verse asks for {reward}something from it, and kind words{/reward}, out of compassion.
now: Bonus day at work, and the cleaner who has no bonus is in the room. The wedding where the poor cousin watches the gifts pile up. {trap}People notice when they are left out.{/trap} {idea}A small gift and a warm word can change how someone remembers that day.{/idea}
old: If they have no right to it, I owe them nothing.
new: The people who are present but left out are a chance for my kindness.
try: Next time you receive something good, share a small part with someone who received nothing.

title: Imagine it is your own children left behind.
subtitle: Treat others' children as you would want yours treated
then: Ibn Abbas explained this as speaking to anyone at the bedside of a dying man who is making an unfair will. {idea}Fear Allah, and steer him toward fairness, as you would want for your own children.{/idea} When Sa'd fell ill, the Prophet ﷺ told him: {reward}it is better to leave your heirs well off than leave them begging from people.{/reward}
now: You are the teacher of a child whose parent just died. You are the uncle in charge of the family estate. You are the manager of the new hire who has nobody. {idea}Picture your own child in their place, with no one to speak up.{/idea} Then decide.
old: Other people's children are their family's concern, not mine.
new: The fairness I want for my own children is the fairness I owe everyone else's.
try: Do one small thing today for a child who is not yours: a word of praise, help with homework, a smile.

title: What looks like a meal is really fire.
subtitle: The true nature of what is taken unjustly

picture.label: What it seems vs what it is

then: The verses before asked guardians to be fair. This one shows the reality behind unfair gain: {trap}what is taken from orphans wrongly is fire, not food.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ listed {trap}consuming an orphan's wealth{/trap} among the seven great destructive sins.
now: The extra you quietly kept from a shared fund. The small cut from money meant for someone vulnerable. {trap}It can feel like nothing.{/trap} The verse asks you to see it for what it is, while there is still time to return it. {idea}The door to fix it is open today.{/idea}
old: A small amount taken from someone weak does not really count.
new: What I take unjustly from the weak is not gain. It is harm I carry.
try: If you owe anything to someone who cannot ask for it, return it or start planning how.

title: You do not know who will benefit you most.
subtitle: Trusting the One who divided it
then: After Uhud, the widow of Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi' came to the Prophet ﷺ with her two daughters. {trap}Their uncle had taken everything their father left.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ said Allah would decide, and this verse came. In the old custom only men inherited. {idea}Now every child had a share set by Allah.{/idea} The detailed shares are a science of their own, studied with scholars.
now: Families fight over a house, a car, a few savings. Everyone has a story about who did more, who deserves more, who was the favorite. {trap}It feels like it should be our call.{/trap} The verse says you do not even know whether your parent or your child will be of more benefit to you. {reward}That is why the division belongs to Allah.{/reward}
old: I know best who in my family deserves what.
new: Allah sees what I cannot, so His division is wiser than my favorites.
try: If you are unsure about inheritance in your family, ask a trusted scholar instead of guessing.

title: A will is not a weapon.
subtitle: Last wishes that cause no harm

row.title: settle scores
sub: cut out the one I resent

row.title: without harm
sub: no one wronged by my wishes

then: This verse continues the shares, naming husbands, wives, and brothers and sisters. Woven through it is one condition: {idea}a will made without causing harm.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains this as {trap}not depriving a rightful heir or adding to someone's fixed portion.{/trap} The verse ends by calling Allah Knowing and Forbearing.
now: You hear of someone who changed their will after a family argument. Or who quietly moved everything to one child. {trap}Last words can be used to punish.{/trap} {idea}Your final wishes are one of your last deeds, and Allah sees them.{/idea}
old: What I leave behind is mine to use however I want, even to make a point.
new: My last wishes should leave no one wronged, because they are deeds too.
try: Write down any debts you owe today, even small ones, so they will not be forgotten.

title: A fair final act can crown a whole life.
subtitle: Staying within the limits Allah set

row.title: a fair will
sub: can make the last deed the best

then: After laying out the shares, the verse calls them {idea}the limits of Allah.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ said a person may do good for seventy years and then be unjust in his will, or do wrong for years and then be fair in his will, {reward}so his final deed becomes his best.{/reward}
now: You think of your life as the big things: the job, the prayers, the kids raised. But the last decisions matter too. The calls you make when you are old or sick. {reward}It is never too late for a fair act to be the one you are remembered by.{/reward}
old: Only the big parts of my life count. The end is just paperwork.
new: Keeping Allah's limits, even in the paperwork at the end, can be the success that crowns a life.
try: Think of one decision you are putting off that affects others. Make it fair, and make it soon.

title: Overriding Allah's division is disputing His judgment.
subtitle: The other side of the same limits
then: This verse is the mirror of the one before. Ibn Kathir explains that whoever {trap}changes what Allah ordained, by tricks and plots{/trap}, is in effect disputing Allah's judgment. The warning is serious because {idea}the ones harmed are often those too weak to object.{/idea}
now: The sibling who signs papers while the others are not looking. The relative who pressures the grieving widow to sign. {trap}It can all feel like normal family business.{/trap} {idea}Before you push for more than your share, remember who drew the lines.{/idea}
old: Bending the rules a little in family money is normal.
new: When I bend what Allah divided, I am arguing with Him, not with my family.
try: If you have ever taken more than your fair share in a family matter, talk to someone about setting it right.

title: Four witnesses: a very high bar before accusing.
subtitle: Guarding people from careless accusation
then: This verse came early in Madinah, in a society reshaping how it dealt with serious wrongdoing. Ibn Kathir notes it was an early stage, and that {idea}Allah later made another way, as the verse itself promised.{/idea} The verse asks for {reward}four witnesses{/reward} before anything happens. The rulings themselves are for scholars and courts, not for individuals.
now: A screenshot is passed around. Someone says they heard something about a woman at the mosque. {trap}It takes one message to ruin a name.{/trap} The verse sets the bar so high that {idea}rumor counts for nothing.{/idea} That is your cue to stay silent too.
old: If many people are saying it, it is probably true.
new: Without clear proof, I have no right to repeat it.
try: The next time a rumor about someone reaches you, do not forward it. Delete it.

title: If they turned back, stop reminding them.
subtitle: Letting go after real repentance

row.title: turn away from it
sub: as if there was no sin

then: Like the verse before, this was an early stage that later rulings replaced, and those details belong to scholars. What stays is the ending: {idea}if they repent and correct themselves, leave them alone.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says {reward}do not abuse them with words after that, since one who truly repents is like one who has no sin.{/reward}
now: A cousin who once went off the rails is now praying again. A friend who wronged you has changed. But at every family dinner, someone brings up the old story. {trap}The past gets used as a leash.{/trap} {reward}If Allah is Accepting of repentance, who are you to keep the file open?{/reward}
old: People who did something bad should never live it down.
new: If Allah accepts someone's repentance, I should stop holding their past over them.
try: Think of someone whose old mistake you still mention. Decide not to bring it up again.

title: Every sin is done in a moment of not knowing better.
subtitle: The door Allah keeps open to those who return soon

row.title: a wrong done
sub: in ignorance, in a weak moment

row.title: too late for me
sub: I knew what I was doing

then: The Companions used to say that {idea}every sin is committed out of ignorance{/idea}, even a deliberate one. And "soon" was explained generously: Ikrimah said {reward}all of this life is soon.{/reward} The Prophet ﷺ said Allah accepts a servant's repentance until the soul reaches the throat.
now: You did something last night you said you would never do again. Now the shame says: you knew better, there is no point. {trap}That voice sounds humble, but it shuts the door.{/trap} {reward}The verse opens it. Turn back today.{/reward}
old: I knew it was wrong and did it anyway, so I cannot be forgiven.
new: Every sin is a lapse of knowing better, and Allah accepts those who return while they still can.
try: Before you sleep tonight, sincerely ask Allah's forgiveness for one specific thing.

title: Saying I repent now, at the very last moment.
subtitle: Why the door should not be left to the end
then: The previous verse opened the door wide. This one shows where it closes. Ibn Kathir explains that once {trap}death is actually present and the soul is being drawn out{/trap}, the chance to repent has passed. The verse speaks of those who kept going until that moment. {idea}The lesson is to turn back while there is time.{/idea}
now: You tell yourself you will sort it out when you are older, after the wedding, after this job. {trap}None of us is promised the next decade, or the next week.{/trap} {idea}The best day to come back is the one you are in.{/idea}
old: I have plenty of time to change before the end.
new: I do not know when my time ends, so the right time to turn back is now.
try: Pick one habit you have been planning to quit someday. Take the first step today.

title: Maybe what you dislike holds much good.
subtitle: Living with kindness, even through dislike

row.title: inheritance
sub: his male relatives decide for her

key.label: When you dislike something in them

row.title: much good
sub: you may not see it yet

then: Ibn Abbas described a custom: when a man died, {trap}his male relatives could do what they wished with his widow{/trap}, as if she were part of his estate. This verse ended that and said: {idea}live with them in kindness.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ said the best of you is the best to his family, and he would race with A'ishah and laugh with his wives.
now: You are irritated with your spouse again. The same habit, the same argument. {trap}Your mind starts keeping a list of everything wrong.{/trap} The verse says: maybe the thing you dislike is where Allah has placed a lot of good. {reward}If one trait annoys you, another one you love is right beside it.{/reward}
old: If something about them bothers me, I am allowed to be cold about it.
new: Kindness is my part even when I dislike something, and Allah may put good right there.
try: Tell someone at home one thing you appreciate about them today, out loud.

title: Even a heap of gold, once given, stays given.
subtitle: Not taking back gifts when love ends
then: The verse imagines a man moving on to another marriage who wants back what he gave his first wife. {trap}Would you take it unjustly, as a plain sin?{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes the verse shows a gift could be very large, and that Umar later changed his view about limiting it. {idea}What was given stays hers.{/idea}
now: A relationship ends badly. Suddenly there is a list: the ring, the phone, the money I spent on you. {trap}Hurt makes you want to take everything back.{/trap} {idea}A gift does not become a loan just because love faded.{/idea}
old: If it ended, I have the right to get back what I gave.
new: What I gave with an open hand stays given, even when things end.
try: Let go of one thing you once gave someone and still secretly want back.

title: After all that closeness, how could you take it back?
subtitle: Marriage as a solemn covenant

row.title: it is over, so we are even

then: This continues the verse before, about a man who wants back what he gave his wife when the marriage ends. The verse does not argue with numbers. It asks a human question: {idea}how could you take it, after you have been so close, and she took from you a solemn covenant?{/idea} {trap}Closeness should make you more generous, not less.{/trap}
now: The breakup, the divorce, the friendship that fell apart. Suddenly you want to count everything. {trap}The years of trust start to look like an invoice.{/trap} The verse asks you to remember what you shared. {reward}Ending with dignity honors the bond you once made.{/reward}
old: When something ends, I can treat the other person like a stranger.
new: A bond that was once close still asks me to be decent when it ends.
try: Think of someone you parted with badly. Say a quiet prayer for their good.

title: What has passed is past. Now the line is drawn.
subtitle: Ending an old custom without condemning the past
then: The surah was replacing old customs of the pre-Islamic period with new ones. This verse ends a practice the Arabs had known. It calls it {trap}shameful, hateful, and an evil way.{/trap} Yet it adds {idea}except what has already passed{/idea}, drawing the line from that day forward.
now: You learn that something you did for years, maybe something your whole family did, was wrong. {trap}It is tempting to either defend it or drown in guilt.{/trap} The verse shows another way: {reward}name it clearly, and change from today.{/reward}
old: If I did it for years, either it was fine or I am beyond help.
new: Allah lets the past be the past when I change course today.
try: Name one old habit you now know is wrong. Decide on one step to change it this week.

title: Some bonds are kept sacred by drawing a line.
subtitle: The protected circle of family
then: Ibn Abbas said this verse names {idea}seven kinds of relatives by blood and seven by marriage{/idea} who can never be married. The Prophet ﷺ added that {reward}nursing creates the same bond as birth.{/reward} The exact details are a matter for scholars. The verse ends: Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
now: Think of the people at a family gathering: your aunt, your stepdaughter, your mother-in-law, the woman who nursed you as a baby. {reward}Allah made them a circle where trust can be total.{/reward} {idea}Some relationships are protected precisely because they are off limits.{/idea}
old: Rules about family relations just limit people.
new: These lines make the family a place of safety and trust.
try: Call one older relative from this circle, an aunt or a milk relative, and just ask how they are.

title: Seeking chastity, not just desire.
subtitle: The intention behind a marriage
then: After listing who cannot be married, the verse calls this {idea}the decree of Allah upon you{/idea} and opens the rest. It names the purpose: {reward}seeking chastity, not unlawful relations.{/reward} It speaks of giving women their due, and of mutual agreement after that. Its legal details, debated by scholars, are not for this card.
now: Dating apps, endless options, talk about "keeping things casual." {trap}Relationships can become about what you get.{/trap} The verse asks a different question: {idea}are you looking to protect someone, and yourself, in a real commitment?{/idea}
old: Relationships are mainly about what I want and feel.
new: Seeking a spouse is about building a protected bond, and giving the other their full due.
try: If you are seeking marriage, write down why, in one honest sentence.

title: Allah knows your faith. You are from one another.
subtitle: Status does not measure a person
then: This verse speaks about a man without the means to marry, in a society with free people and servants. Its legal content is for scholars. Woven into it are two lines that cut through status: {idea}Allah knows best your faith, and you are from one another.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says people see only the outside, while Allah knows the inside. It ends: {reward}patience is better for you.{/reward}
now: Your family judges a proposal by salary, surname, or neighborhood. You catch yourself thinking someone is beneath you because of their job. {trap}Status quietly decides who is worth respect.{/trap} {idea}Allah knows who carries real faith, and you cannot see it.{/idea}
old: I can judge a person's worth by their position and background.
new: Allah alone knows the faith inside a person, and we are all from one another.
try: Greet someone today whose job people tend to overlook, and thank them by name.

title: Allah wants to make it clear for you.
subtitle: The purpose behind all these rulings
then: After many verses of family law, Allah steps back and says why. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}Allah explains what He allowed and prohibited, and shows the righteous ways of those before you.{/idea} And then: {reward}He wants to accept your repentance.{/reward}
now: You read the long rules about family and money and feel overwhelmed. {trap}It can feel like religion is just a list of things you will get wrong.{/trap} The verse tells you the intention behind it: {reward}clarity, guidance, and a way back when you slip.{/reward}
old: Religious rules are mostly about catching me out.
new: Allah gave me clear guidance because He wants to guide me and forgive me.
try: Learn one ruling you are unsure about from a trusted teacher this week.

title: Two pulls: one toward forgiveness, one toward drifting far.
subtitle: Who wants what for you
then: The verse repeats what Allah wants: {reward}to accept your repentance.{/reward} Then it names the opposite pull. Those who follow their desires want you to {trap}swerve far off the path{/trap}, not just a little. Ibn Kathir describes it as wanting you to take the path of falsehood instead of the truth.
now: The friend who says "everybody does it." The feed that keeps showing you one more video. {trap}Each step feels small. The direction is what matters.{/trap} {idea}Notice who benefits from you drifting.{/idea}
old: A few small compromises will not change who I am.
new: Some voices want me to drift far, while Allah wants to bring me back.
try: Unfollow or mute one account that pulls you somewhere you do not want to go.

title: You were made weak, so Allah made it lighter.
subtitle: Ease built into the guidance
then: After the rulings on marriage, the verse says: {reward}Allah wants to lighten things for you{/reward}, because {idea}man was created weak.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains this is why the commands were made easy. Tawus said the weakness meant here is especially with desire.
now: You set big goals for yourself and keep failing. The same struggle with your eyes, your temper, your phone. {trap}You feel like the only one who cannot hold it together.{/trap} {reward}Allah already knew, and built ease into His guidance for you.{/reward}
old: If I struggle, I must not be a real believer.
new: Allah knows I am weak, and His guidance was made light for exactly that reason.
try: Pick the easiest good habit you can keep, even two minutes a day, and start it today.

title: Do not destroy yourselves. Allah is Merciful to you.
subtitle: Honest dealing and protecting life
then: The verse forbids taking each other's wealth by false means, except {idea}trade by mutual consent.{/idea} Then: {trap}do not kill yourselves.{/trap} On a freezing night, Amr bin Al-As feared that bathing in icy water would kill him, so he used dust instead and recalled this verse. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ smiled and said nothing against it.{/reward}
now: The hidden fee in your invoice. The sale where you knew the buyer did not understand. And the darker nights, when you feel you cannot go on. {reward}The verse ends with Allah's mercy toward you.{/reward} {idea}Your life matters to Him.{/idea}
old: My life and my dealings are only my own business.
new: Allah protects my life and asks me to deal fairly, out of mercy for me.
try: If you are struggling with dark thoughts, tell one person you trust today, or call a helpline.

title: Knowing it is wrong and doing it anyway.
subtitle: A warning about defiant wrongdoing
then: This warning follows the verse about false gain and taking life. Ibn Kathir explains it is about someone who does it {trap}through aggression and injustice, knowing it is forbidden, yet still daring to do it.{/trap} He calls it {idea}a stern warning and a truthful promise{/idea}, for anyone who hears with understanding.
now: You know the deal is dishonest. You know the words will wound. And there is a moment when you decide to do it anyway. {idea}That moment is where this verse speaks.{/idea} {reward}It is also the moment you can still stop.{/reward}
old: Everyone cuts corners. Allah will overlook it.
new: Doing wrong knowingly and defiantly is serious, and I can still choose to stop.
try: Notice the next time you are about to do something you know is wrong. Pause and walk away.

title: Keep away from the big ones, and the small are wiped.
subtitle: A promise of forgiveness and a noble entrance

row.title: guard the big lines
sub: and trust His mercy for the rest

then: Ibn Mas'ud counted this among five verses of this surah he loved more than the world and all in it. {reward}If you avoid the major sins, Allah wipes away the lesser ones.{/reward} The Prophet ﷺ said that one Friday prayer to the next wipes out what is between them, {idea}as long as major sins are avoided.{/idea}
now: You keep a mental list of every small failing: the snapped word, the late prayer, the scroll you should not have done. {trap}It can make you feel there is no point trying.{/trap} The verse gives you a clear focus. {idea}Hold the big lines firmly, and keep coming back to Allah for the rest.{/idea}
old: Since I keep slipping in small things, I might as well give up.
new: If I hold firm on the big lines, Allah promises to wipe away the small slips.
try: Go to this Friday's prayer early and quietly, and ask Allah to wipe the week's slips.

title: Stop wishing for their portion. Ask Allah for yours.
subtitle: From envy to asking

row.title: Allah, give me from Your bounty

then: Umm Salamah said to the Prophet ﷺ that men go out to battle and receive more inheritance, while women do not. The verse answered: {trap}do not wish for what Allah gave others over you.{/trap} {idea}Each, man and woman, has a share of what they earned.{/idea} Ibn Kathir paraphrases: wishing does not change the decree, so {reward}ask Me of My favor and I will grant it.{/reward}
now: Your colleague's promotion. Your friend's wedding photos. Your sibling's easy life. {trap}You scroll and feel smaller with every post.{/trap} The verse redirects the longing. {reward}Do not stare at their portion. Turn and ask Allah for good in yours.{/reward}
old: Seeing what others have makes me feel I have been shortchanged.
new: My share is earned and known to Allah, and I can ask Him for more of His bounty.
try: When you next feel envy, stop and make a dua for that person and for yourself.

title: Keep the promises you already made.
subtitle: Pledges of brotherhood, witnessed by Allah
then: When the emigrants came to Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ paired them with the Ansar as brothers, and at first they inherited from each other. Ibn Abbas explained that this verse set heirs from family, while {idea}the pledge stayed valid for help, support, and sincere advice.{/idea} {reward}Allah is Witness over all things.{/reward}
now: The friend who promised to be there for you, and you for them. The colleague who took you in when you were new. {trap}Over time, these promises quietly fade.{/trap} {idea}Allah witnessed what you pledged.{/idea} Keep showing up.
old: Old promises of friendship do not really bind me anymore.
new: The bonds I pledged before Allah still ask for my help and good advice.
try: Message a friend who once stood by you, and ask if there is anything they need.

title: Responsibility in the home answers to the Most High.
subtitle: Care, provision, and accountability before Allah

key.label: The line the verse ends on

row.title: I am in charge
sub: so I can do as I like

then: This verse speaks about roles and conflict in marriage, and its rulings need qualified scholars, not a card. Ibn Kathir highlights how it closes: {idea}Allah is Most High, Most Great.{/idea} He explains this reminds men that {trap}if they wrong their wives without right{/trap}, Allah is the wife's Protector. The Prophet ﷺ said a wife's right is to be fed and clothed as you are, and never cursed.
now: You pay the rent, you make the big calls, people at home depend on you. {trap}It is easy to let responsibility turn into control.{/trap} The verse ends by pointing above you. {idea}Whatever authority you hold at home, you answer to Allah for how you use it.{/idea}
old: Being responsible for my family means I have the final word on everything.
new: Responsibility at home is a trust, and Allah, Most High, watches how I carry it.
try: Ask the person you share a home with: is there something I do that makes life harder for you?

title: If both want to fix it, Allah brings them together.
subtitle: Sending wise people to mend a rift
then: After speaking of conflict, the verse describes a deeper rift between spouses. {idea}Send a fair person from each family to look into it.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes that Allah gives preference to staying together, which is why He says: {reward}if they both want reconciliation, Allah will bring it about.{/reward}
now: The cold silence at home has lasted weeks. Both families have opinions, and some are only pouring fuel. {trap}Everyone wants to be proven right.{/trap} The verse asks for one wise, fair voice on each side, and one thing from you: {reward}really want to mend it.{/reward}
old: If our marriage is struggling, nobody else should get involved.
new: A fair voice from each side, and a sincere wish to mend, opens the way for Allah's help.
try: If a rift is growing in your home, think of one wise, fair person you could ask for help.

title: Worship Allah alone, then widen the circle of kindness.
subtitle: From parents to the stranger beside you
then: The verse ties worship of Allah directly to doing good to a long line of people, from parents to servants. The Prophet ﷺ said {idea}Jibril kept urging me about the neighbor until I thought he would make him an heir.{/idea} In his final illness, {reward}he kept repeating: the prayer, the prayer, and those under your care.{/reward}
now: The neighbor whose name you never learned. The coworker on the next desk. The delivery rider at your door. {trap}It is easy to be warm to family and invisible to everyone else.{/trap} {idea}The verse draws them all into your worship.{/idea}
old: My religious duty is to Allah and my family. Everyone else is extra.
new: Worshiping Allah includes being good to the neighbor, the stranger, and the one serving me.
try: Take a small gift or plate of food to the neighbor whose door is closest to yours.

title: Stingy, and teaching others to be stingy.
subtitle: Hiding the favors Allah gave you

row.title: let it show
sub: the effect of His favor on you

then: Right after listing the people to be kind to, the verse turns to those who {trap}hold back, urge others to hold back, and hide what Allah gave them.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ asked, what disease is worse than stinginess? He also said {reward}when Allah blesses a servant, He loves to see its effect on him.{/reward}
now: Your friend wants to donate, and you say: you have bills, be careful. You downplay your raise so no one asks for help. {trap}Stinginess spreads quietly through advice.{/trap} {idea}Let Allah's favor show in how you give.{/idea}
old: Being careful with money is always wise, so I tell others to hold back too.
new: Hiding and hoarding Allah's blessings is ingratitude. Letting them flow shows thanks.
try: Give something today to one person from the list in the last verse, and tell no one.

title: Giving to be seen has a bad companion.
subtitle: When generosity is for show
then: The verse before named the stingy. This one names the opposite mistake: {trap}spending to be seen.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ described a wealthy man who claims he spent everywhere for Allah, and is told: {trap}you did it so people would say he is generous, and it was said.{/trap} {idea}Shaytan makes the show look like a good deed.{/idea}
now: You post the charity receipt. You make sure the right people see you hand over the envelope. {trap}The likes feel like reward.{/trap} {idea}Ask yourself who the giving was really for.{/idea}
old: As long as the money helps someone, it does not matter why I give it.
new: Giving for show takes its reward from people. Giving for Allah keeps it with Him.
try: Make your next donation completely private. No post, no mention.

title: What would it have cost them?
subtitle: The gentle question after the warning

row.title: believe
sub: in Allah and the Last Day

then: After naming the stingy and the show-offs, the verse asks softly: {idea}what harm would it have done them to believe and to spend from what Allah gave them?{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains: what harm if they {reward}replaced showing off with sincerity{/reward}? And Allah knows their intentions.
now: You hesitate before giving. You worry what you will lose. You overthink whether anyone will notice. {idea}The verse asks you: what would it actually cost you?{/idea} {reward}What is given from what Allah gave you is never truly lost.{/reward}
old: Giving sincerely costs me money and recognition.
new: Faith and sincere giving cost me nothing real, and Allah knows my heart.
try: Give something small today purely for Allah, and notice that you lost nothing.

title: Not an atom of injustice. Every good multiplied.
subtitle: Allah's perfect fairness and generosity
then: Ibn Mas'ud counted this verse among the five in this surah he loved more than the world. {idea}Allah does not wrong anyone even by a speck of dust.{/idea} In the hadith of intercession, Allah says to bring out of the Fire anyone with {reward}even the smallest speck of faith in their heart.{/reward}
now: The smile at the cashier. The bag you carried for an old man. The prayer no one saw. {trap}It all feels too small to matter.{/trap} {reward}Nothing is lost with Allah. He multiplies it.{/reward}
old: Small good deeds do not really count for much.
new: Allah misses nothing, not even an atom, and He multiplies every good I do.
try: Do three tiny good deeds today and trust that each one is seen.

title: The verse that brought tears to the Prophet's eyes.
subtitle: A witness from every nation
then: The Prophet ﷺ once asked Ibn Mas'ud to recite to him, saying he loved to hear the Quran from others. Ibn Mas'ud recited this surah until he reached this verse. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ said: stop now.{/idea} Ibn Mas'ud looked and {reward}saw that his eyes were full of tears.{/reward}
now: You read verses quickly, scrolling past to finish a page. {trap}They barely land.{/trap} Here is the Prophet ﷺ, who received this Quran, stopped by one line about the Day of witnesses. {idea}Let one verse stop you today.{/idea}
old: Reading the Quran is about finishing pages.
new: One verse truly heard can move the heart more than many pages rushed.
try: Ask someone to recite a short passage to you, and just listen.

title: Wishing the earth would swallow you, and hiding nothing.
subtitle: When every word is known
then: This verse continues the scene of witnesses. Those who denied and disobeyed the Messenger will {trap}wish the earth would be leveled over them{/trap}, out of the shame of that gathering. Yet {idea}they will not hide a single statement from Allah.{/idea} Ibn Kathir links it to the Day when a person sees what their hands sent ahead.
now: The message you deleted. The search history you cleared. The thing you said that no one else heard. {trap}It feels hidden.{/trap} {idea}Before Allah, nothing is.{/idea} {reward}That is a reason to fix things now, while you still can.{/reward}
old: If no one finds out, it is as if it never happened.
new: Nothing I say or do is hidden from Allah, so I should mend it while I can.
try: Think of one thing you are hiding that harms someone. Take one step to make it right.

title: Come to prayer knowing what you are saying.
subtitle: A present mind, and an easy way when water is missing
then: Before alcohol was fully banned, Ali described a meal where some drank, then {trap}the man leading prayer recited a surah wrongly, reversing its meaning.{/trap} This verse came: {idea}do not approach prayer until you know what you are saying.{/idea} It also gave an easier way when water cannot be found. Its rulings are for scholars to explain. It ends: {reward}Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving.{/reward}
now: You start the prayer while your mind is still in the argument, the inbox, the game. {trap}You finish and cannot remember what you recited.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ said if you grow sleepy in prayer, rest first, so you know what you are saying. {idea}Come with your mind, not only your body.{/idea}
old: As long as I get through the prayer, it counts.
new: Prayer is a conversation, so I should come knowing what I am saying.
try: In your next prayer, choose one phrase and think about its meaning as you say it.

title: Given guidance, and trading it for error.
subtitle: When knowledge does not lead to following
then: In Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ faced opposition from some who already had scripture, as the surah introduction describes. The verse points to people {reward}given a portion of the Book{/reward} who {trap}bought error with it, and wanted the believers to lose the way too.{/trap}
now: You know the verses about anger, about honesty, about prayer. You have watched the lectures. {trap}Yet knowing has not changed what you do.{/trap} {idea}Knowledge given is a trust. Do not trade it away.{/idea}
old: Knowing a lot about religion means I am on the right path.
new: Knowledge only guides me if I follow it instead of trading it for what I want.
try: Take one thing you already know you should do, and do it today.

title: Allah is enough as your Protector and Helper.
subtitle: When people work against you
then: The young community in Madinah faced pressure from many sides. After warning about those who wanted them to lose the way, the verse reassures them: {idea}Allah knows your enemies best.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains He is {reward}a sufficient Protector for those who seek refuge with Him, and a sufficient Helper for those who ask His help.{/reward}
now: The colleague undermining you in meetings. The relative spreading stories. You lie awake planning how to defend yourself. {trap}It feels like it all depends on you.{/trap} {reward}Allah sees what they do better than you, and He is enough.{/reward}
old: I have to watch every move my opponents make, or I will lose.
new: Allah knows who is against me, and He is enough as my Protector and Helper.
try: Tonight, hand one worry about a person over to Allah in dua, and then sleep.

title: We hear and we obey would have been better.
subtitle: Twisting words versus sincere listening
then: The verse describes some in Madinah who {trap}twisted words from their meaning{/trap}, and spoke to the Prophet ﷺ with phrases that sounded polite but carried mockery. It then shows a better way: {idea}we hear and we obey, and help us understand.{/idea} That, it says, {reward}would have been better and more upright.{/reward}
now: Someone gives you advice and you say, sure, fine, with a tone that says the opposite. You quote a verse with a twist to win an argument. {trap}It is easy to listen only to reply.{/trap} {idea}Try saying: I hear you, help me understand.{/idea}
old: I can listen politely and still do what I want.
new: Sincere listening sounds like: we hear, we obey, and help us understand.
try: In your next disagreement, say: help me understand what you mean. Then listen.

title: Believe what confirms what you already have.
subtitle: A call that moved Ka'b to believe
then: The verse calls those given scripture to believe in the Quran, which {idea}confirms what is already with them{/idea}, and warns of what may come if they turn away. Ka'b al-Ahbar had told Umar he was not ready. Later, in Hims, he heard someone recite this verse and said: {reward}I believe, my Lord. I accept Islam, my Lord.{/reward}
now: You keep saying "later" to something you know is true. Later I will pray properly. Later I will make that change. {trap}Later can quietly become never.{/trap} {idea}Like Ka'b, when the verse reaches you, answer it.{/idea}
old: I will act on what I know when I am ready.
new: When the truth reaches me, the time to answer is now.
try: Name one thing you keep postponing for "later" and do the first part of it today.

title: Everything else He may forgive. Guard the one thing.
subtitle: The vastness of forgiveness, and its one wall

key.label: What Allah says in the hadith

then: Ibn Mas'ud counted this among the five verses of this surah he loved most. Ibn Umar said they used to hold back from asking forgiveness for those with major sins {reward}until they heard this verse.{/reward} The Prophet ﷺ reported Allah saying: if you meet Me with {reward}an earth full of sins, without associating anything with Me, I will meet you with an earth full of forgiveness.{/reward}
now: You feel your sins are too many, too big, too repeated. {trap}You start to think your case is closed.{/trap} The verse shows the door is wider than your fear. {idea}Hold on to Allah alone, and keep asking.{/idea}
old: My sins are too many for Allah to forgive.
new: Allah's forgiveness is vast for those who keep their worship for Him alone.
try: Say la ilaha illa Allah slowly, meaning it, and then ask Allah to forgive you.

title: You cannot declare yourself pure. Allah purifies.
subtitle: Self-praise versus Allah's judgment

row.title: a thread in a date stone

then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah said this verse was about people who claimed {trap}they were Allah's children and His beloved{/trap}, sure of their own goodness. The verse answers: {idea}Allah purifies whom He wills{/idea}, since He knows the true reality of things. And no one is wronged even by {reward}the thread in a date stone.{/reward}
now: You compare your prayers to someone else's and feel safe. You call your group, your mosque, your family the good ones. {trap}Self-praise feels like security.{/trap} {idea}Only Allah knows who is truly pure.{/idea}
old: I am clearly one of the good people.
new: Only Allah can declare who is pure, so I keep working instead of praising myself.
try: Catch yourself the next time you compare yourself favorably to someone. Make a dua for them instead.

title: Look how they put their own claims in Allah's mouth.
subtitle: Inventing a lie about Allah

row.title: self-praise
sub: we are safe, we are loved

then: This continues the verse before. Claiming purity for yourself and saying {trap}the Fire will barely touch us{/trap} is, in effect, inventing a lie about Allah. Ibn Kathir notes they relied on the good deeds of their forefathers, yet {idea}the deeds of fathers do not save the children.{/idea} Each earns their own.
now: Your grandfather was a scholar. Your family has always been religious. You assume Allah is pleased with you because of who you come from. {trap}It is a comfortable story.{/trap} {idea}Allah will look at what you did.{/idea}
old: Coming from a good family means I am on the safe side.
new: My family's goodness does not carry me. My own deeds do.
try: Do one good deed today that is only yours, not your family's habit.

title: Calling the wrong side better guided, to win an ally.
subtitle: When people trade the truth for allies
then: Ikrimah reported that two leaders who had scripture visited Makkah. The Quraysh asked them to judge between themselves and the Prophet ﷺ. Wanting allies against him, {trap}they told the idol worshippers: you are more righteous and better guided.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes this led toward the Battle of the Trench, and {idea}Allah protected the believers.{/idea}
now: A friend asks you who was right in a fight. You know the answer, but your friend is useful to you. Your boss asks your opinion, and you say what keeps you safe. {trap}Telling people what they want to hear feels harmless.{/trap} {idea}Say what is true, even when it costs you an ally.{/idea}
old: Sometimes I have to bend the truth to keep the right people on my side.
new: Calling wrong right to win allies is a betrayal of what I know.
try: The next time someone asks your honest opinion, give it kindly and truthfully.

title: Those whose help they sought could not help them.
subtitle: No helper apart from Allah
then: This verse follows directly from the last. Those who praised the wrong side to gain allies were far from Allah's mercy. Ibn Kathir explains they {trap}sought the help of the idol worshippers{/trap}, yet {idea}whoever Allah turns away from will find no helper.{/idea} The allies they courted could not save them.
now: You flatter the right people, join the right group, stay quiet when it is convenient, all to feel protected. {trap}It feels like insurance.{/trap} {idea}No one can help you if you have walked away from Allah.{/idea}
old: Having powerful people on my side keeps me safe.
new: Real help comes only from Allah, and no alliance replaces Him.
try: Think of whose approval you work hardest for. Ask yourself whether it pleases Allah.

title: Even owning a kingdom, they would not share a speck.
subtitle: How stinginess grows with power

row.title: not a speck
sub: the dot on a date stone

then: The verse asks a pointed question: do they have a share of the dominion? Even if they did, {trap}they would not give people the speck on the back of a date stone.{/trap} Ibn Kathir links it to another verse: if you held the treasures of Allah's mercy, {idea}you would hold back for fear of spending.{/idea}
now: You tell yourself you will give once the mortgage is paid, once the business grows, once you feel secure. {trap}But the more you have, the more you worry about losing it.{/trap} {idea}Generosity is not a size. It is a habit you start now.{/idea}
old: I will be generous once I have more.
new: If I do not give a little now, more will not make me give.
try: Give a small amount today, even if it feels like too little to matter.

title: Envying someone for what Allah chose to give them.
subtitle: Blessings are His to give

row.title: Allah gives
sub: as He gave the family of Ibrahim

then: Ibn Kathir explains this was about envy of the Prophet ﷺ for the prophethood Allah gave him. Ibn Abbas described the feeling as {trap}we are the worthy ones, not the rest of the people.{/trap} The verse answers: {idea}Allah already gave the family of Ibrahim the Book, wisdom, and a great kingdom.{/idea} The gift was always His to give.
now: Your cousin gets the scholarship. Your coworker, newer than you, gets the role. {trap}A voice says: that should have been mine.{/trap} {idea}Allah gives as He wills, and envy only burns the one who holds it.{/idea}
old: When someone else gets what I wanted, it is unfair.
new: What Allah gives others is His choice, and I can ask Him for my own share.
try: Congratulate, sincerely, one person whose blessing you secretly envied.

title: The same gift, two responses.
subtitle: Some believed, some turned away
then: The family of Ibrahim was given prophets, books, and kingship. Yet {idea}some of them believed in it{/idea}, and {trap}some turned away from it and kept others from it.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes they disputed even with their own prophets. The verse closes with a sober warning about the Fire.
now: Two siblings raised in the same home, the same mosque, the same lessons. One holds on, one drifts. {trap}Blessings do not guarantee a response.{/trap} {idea}What reaches you is a gift. What you do with it is yours.{/idea}
old: Growing up around faith means I will naturally stay on it.
new: The gift of guidance asks for my own response, every day.
try: Think of one blessing of faith you were given. Thank Allah for it by name.

title: A punishment that never wears off.
subtitle: Why the warning is so serious

row.title: it will fade
sub: I will get used to it

then: Ibn Kathir explains this verse describes those who rejected Allah's signs and blocked the path of His messengers. The verse uses a stark image to show that {trap}the punishment does not dull or wear off.{/trap} It ends: {idea}Allah is Mighty, Wise.{/idea} The next verse immediately turns to the gardens.
now: We get used to pain here. Bad news fades, aches settle. {trap}It is easy to assume everything wears off eventually.{/trap} This verse says some things do not. {reward}That is why the door of return, still open today, is such a mercy.{/reward}
old: Whatever happens after death, I will get used to it.
new: The warning is real and lasting, and that makes today's chance to return precious.
try: Make one sincere dua today asking Allah to protect you from the Fire.

title: A shade so wide a rider cannot cross it in a century.
subtitle: The reward of faith and good deeds
then: Right after the warning, the verse turns to {idea}those who believe and do good.{/idea} Gardens with rivers, forever. Spouses purified of every flaw. And {reward}deep, spreading shade.{/reward} The Prophet ﷺ said there is a tree in Paradise whose shade {reward}a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing.{/reward}
now: A summer afternoon in the city. The heat on the bus, the long walk from the station, no shade anywhere. {trap}You long for one tree.{/trap} {reward}Allah promises shade that never ends{/reward}, for faith joined with good deeds.
old: Paradise feels too far away to motivate me today.
new: Every good deed with faith is a step toward a shade that never ends.
try: On a hot or tiring moment today, remember that shade, and do one good deed for it.

title: He handed back the key of the Ka'bah.
subtitle: Returning trusts and judging fairly
then: On the day Makkah was opened, the Prophet ﷺ took the key of the Ka'bah from Uthman bin Talhah and entered. When he came out, {idea}he was reciting this verse, and he gave the key back to him.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said the verse is for everyone, righteous or not. The Prophet ﷺ also said: {reward}return the trust even to one who betrayed you.{/reward}
now: The borrowed book still on your shelf. The secret a friend told you. The keys to the office. The vote you cast in a meeting. {trap}Small trusts slip easily.{/trap} {idea}Each one has an owner, and Allah hears and sees.{/idea}
old: Trusts are only about money or things I borrowed.
new: Everything placed in my hands is a trust, including secrets, roles, and fairness.
try: Return one thing you have borrowed and kept too long, today.

title: Obedience is only in what is right.
subtitle: When you disagree, return it to Allah and His Messenger
then: Ali reported a commander who, angry with his troops, lit a fire and ordered them in. {trap}They nearly entered.{/trap} A young man said: wait, ask the Messenger first. The Prophet ﷺ later said: {idea}had you entered it, you would never have come out. Obedience is only in what is right.{/idea} The verse adds: {reward}if you disagree, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.{/reward}
now: A team argues over a decision. A family splits over what to do for an elderly parent. {trap}Everyone pulls toward their own opinion.{/trap} The verse gives a calm step: {idea}bring it back to what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ taught.{/idea}
old: Whoever is in charge gets the final word, no matter what.
new: I respect those in charge in what is right, and take disagreements back to Allah and His Messenger.
try: In your next disagreement, ask: what would the Quran and Sunnah say about this? Then look it up together.

title: Shopping for the judge who will rule your way.
subtitle: Claiming faith, but seeking another verdict

row.title: what is true
sub: even if it goes against me

then: Ibn Kathir reports that this verse came about a man who claimed to believe, yet in a dispute {trap}wanted to take his case to someone other than the Prophet ﷺ.{/trap} The verse names the pull behind it: {trap}Shaytan wants to lead them far astray.{/trap} {idea}Its meaning is general for anyone who turns from what Allah sent down.{/idea}
now: You have a family dispute and call only the relative who always agrees with you. You search online until you find the answer you wanted. {trap}It feels like research. It is shopping.{/trap} {idea}Go to the honest source, even if the answer is not yours.{/idea}
old: I can look for the opinion that suits me and call it guidance.
new: Real faith means taking my case to what is true, not to whoever will agree with me.
try: Next time you need advice, ask someone who will tell you the truth, not just what you want.

title: Invited to the revelation, they turned their backs.
subtitle: When the invitation is to Allah's word itself
then: In Madinah some people claimed faith but, in their disputes, wanted a judge other than the Prophet ﷺ. When told to come to what Allah revealed, {trap}they turned away in arrogance{/trap}. The tafsir contrasts this with the believers, whose only answer was {idea}we hear and we obey{/idea}.
now: You ask a question online and get three answers. The one from the Quran and Sunnah is clear but costs you something. The other two are easier. You scroll past the clear one and quote the easy one. {trap}That small scroll past{/trap} is the turning away this verse describes.
old: I take guidance seriously, as long as it agrees with me.
new: The test of faith is how I react when the clear answer is the inconvenient one.
try: Think of one thing you already know Allah asks of you that you keep arguing around. Stop arguing for a day.

title: After the trouble comes, the excuses start.
subtitle: Swearing good intentions once things go wrong

row.title: Need, not conviction
sub: they came because they were stuck

then: The hypocrites who avoided the Prophet's ﷺ judgment would come back {trap}once a disaster hit them because of their own deeds{/trap}. They swore by Allah that they had only wanted goodwill and reconciliation. Ibn Kathir explains they came out of need, not belief.
now: You ignored the advice, made the deal, and it fell apart. Now you call the person who warned you and open with, I was only trying to keep everyone happy. {idea}The honest sentence is shorter: I chose wrong.{/idea}
old: My intentions were good, so the outcome is not really on me.
new: Swearing to good intentions after the fact is often a way to avoid owning the choice.
try: Next time something you chose goes badly, say I got that wrong before any explanation.

title: Allah knows the heart. Your job is the word that reaches it.
subtitle: Leave the hidden to Allah, speak to the soul

row.title: turn aside
sub: do not punish what is hidden

row.title: I judge their hearts
sub: I know what they really mean

row.title: Allah knows hearts
sub: I owe them a sincere word

then: Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that He knows what is in these people's hearts, so {idea}do not punish them for what is hidden{/idea}. Instead, advise them and speak to them, between you and them, {reward}with effective words that might benefit them{/reward}.
now: Your cousin says one thing at family dinners and another behind your back. You could expose him in the family group chat. Or you could leave his heart to Allah and, one evening, say something honest to him alone. {reward}A word meant to reach, not to win.{/reward}
old: If I know someone is fake, I should call them out.
new: The hidden part belongs to Allah. My part is a private, sincere word that could help.
try: If you have been rehearsing a public callout, rewrite it as one kind, private sentence instead.

title: Even after wronging yourself, the door was open.
subtitle: What they could have done instead of excuses
then: Right after the excuses of the hypocrites, Allah describes the other road. Messengers are sent {idea}to be obeyed, by Allah's leave{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says the verse directs sinners, when they err, to come and seek Allah's forgiveness, and {reward}they would find Him forgiving and merciful{/reward}.
now: You snapped at your mother, missed the prayer, said the thing you swore you would not say. The mind starts building a defense. {idea}The verse points to a shorter path: come back and ask.{/idea} The door was open the whole time you were explaining.
old: After what I did, I need a good explanation before I can face Allah.
new: I do not need a defense. I need to turn back, and He is already accepting.
try: Tonight, name one wrong from today to Allah and ask forgiveness for it, with no excuse attached.

title: Faith shows when the ruling goes against you.
subtitle: No resentment inside, not just compliance outside
then: Allah swears by Himself that faith is not complete until people bring their disputes to the Prophet ﷺ and {idea}find no resistance in themselves{/idea} toward his decision. Az-Zubayr thought it came down after a man quarreled over irrigation water and said {trap}is it because he is your cousin?{/trap}
now: You asked for guidance on something that matters to you: money, a family split, a habit. The answer is clear and it is not the one you wanted. You follow it, but you sulk about it for a week. {idea}The verse asks for the inside too, not just the outside.{/idea}
old: As long as I do what is right, it does not matter how I feel about it.
new: Real trust means letting the right answer settle in my heart, not just my actions.
try: Pick one teaching you follow with a grudge. Ask Allah to make your heart content with it.

title: They balked at the easy. What if it had been hard?
subtitle: Doing what you are advised makes you steadier
then: Allah says that if He had commanded these people with something truly hard, {trap}only a few would have done it{/trap}. They were struggling with far less. But if they did what they were advised, it would be {reward}better for them and strengthen their conviction{/reward}.
now: Fajr feels heavy. A kind word to your sibling feels impossible. Paying back a friend on time feels like a sacrifice. {idea}None of it is the hard test the verse imagines.{/idea} And each time you do it anyway, your footing gets a little firmer.
old: What is asked of me is too much.
new: What is asked of me is lighter than it could be, and doing it is what makes me steady.
try: Do the one small thing you have been advised to do and keep putting off. Just once today.

title: The reward would come from Allah's own presence.
subtitle: What doing the advised thing would have earned
then: Continuing from the previous verse: had they done what they were told, Allah says {reward}We would have given them a great reward from Ourselves{/reward}. Ibn Kathir explains the reward as Paradise. The point lands on the people who held back over small things.
now: You cleaned up after everyone at the family gathering and nobody noticed. You covered a colleague's shift and got no thanks. {reward}The verse moves the payment desk.{/reward} It is not their thanks you were waiting on.
old: If no one noticed, it was wasted effort.
new: The reward for obeying comes from Allah Himself, noticed or not.
try: Do one helpful thing today and tell no one about it.

title: Obedience opens the way to more guidance.
subtitle: Acting on what you know brings the next step

row.title: the straight path
sub: in this life and the next

then: The third promise in this chain: had they acted on what they were told, {reward}Allah would have guided them to a straight path{/reward}. Ibn Kathir adds, {idea}in this life and the Hereafter{/idea}. Guidance is pictured as something that follows action.
now: You keep waiting for clarity about your career, your marriage, your faith, before changing anything. Meanwhile you already know the one thing you should be doing this week. {idea}Doing it is how the path gets clearer.{/idea}
old: I will act once I am sure where this is going.
new: Acting on what I already know is how I get guided to what I do not.
try: Write down one thing you already know is right for you. Do the first part of it today.

title: Obey, and you end up in the best company.
subtitle: The friends waiting for those who follow

row.title: I will never see him
sub: he will be with the Prophets

row.title: with those you love
sub: through obeying Allah and His Messenger ﷺ

then: Ibn Kathir reports that an Ansari man came to the Prophet ﷺ sad, afraid that in Paradise {trap}he would be separated from him{/trap}. This verse came down and the Prophet ﷺ sent him the good news. Elsewhere he said, {reward}one is with those whom he loves{/reward}.
now: Think about who you spend your evenings with, on screen and off. The verse paints a different circle: Prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, the righteous. {reward}And excellent are those as companions.{/reward} Every act of obedience is a step toward that table.
old: People like the Prophets are far above me. I will never be near them.
new: Obedience and love can place me in their company, even if my deeds are small.
try: Spend ten minutes today reading about one of the righteous you love, and ask Allah to join you with them.

title: That company is a gift, not a wage.
subtitle: Allah knows who deserves His bounty

row.title: a favor
sub: given by One who knows you

then: After promising the company of the Prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, Allah closes: {reward}that is the bounty from Allah{/reward}. Ibn Kathir reports Anas hoping to be raised with those he loved {idea}even without deeds like theirs{/idea}.
now: You compare your worship to someone else's and feel either proud or hopeless. Both miss the point. {reward}The seat is a gift.{/reward} And Allah knows exactly what your effort cost you, in the quiet hours no one sees.
old: My place with Allah is a score I am keeping.
new: It is His bounty, and He alone knows what my effort really was.
try: Thank Allah today for one good deed you managed, as His gift to you rather than your achievement.

title: Trust in Allah never meant walking in unprepared.
subtitle: Precaution and togetherness as part of faith

row.title: prepare, then trust
sub: precaution is part of the task

then: The young community in Madinah faced real enemies. Allah told the believers to {idea}take their precautions{/idea} and move out in groups or all together. Ibn Kathir explains this as being prepared and supplied, {idea}group after group{/idea}, rather than scattered and careless.
now: You say tawakkul while skipping the revision, the budget, the doctor's appointment. Or you try to carry a family crisis alone when your siblings could share it. {idea}The verse pairs readiness with company.{/idea} Do your part, and do not do it alone.
old: If I really trusted Allah, I would not need to plan.
new: Preparing well and working together are part of trusting Allah, not the opposite.
try: Pick one thing you are facing this week and do one concrete step of preparation for it today.

title: He counted staying away as a blessing.
subtitle: The one who lingers behind and feels lucky
then: Mujahid and others said this was about the hypocrites. One would {trap}linger behind and lure others to do the same{/trap}. When the believers suffered loss, he called his absence a favor from Allah, {idea}unaware of the reward he had missed{/idea}.
now: The community iftar needed volunteers and you stayed home. Later you hear it was chaos and the cooks were up till two. You think, glad I was not there. {idea}The verse asks what you missed, not what you avoided.{/idea}
old: Staying out of the hard thing was smart, even lucky.
new: Avoiding a shared hardship can mean missing a share of its reward.
try: Sign up for one small shared task you have been dodging, at your masjid, work or home.

title: Now that it went well, he wishes he had come.
subtitle: Loyalty that switches on only for the gains

row.title: if only I had been there

then: When the believers received a bounty, the same man would speak {trap}as if there had never been affection between you{/trap}. He wished he had been there, Ibn Kathir says, for his share of the gains. {trap}That was his real aim.{/trap}
now: Your friend's start-up struggled for two years and you kept your distance. Now it is doing well, and you message: we should catch up, I always believed in you. {idea}The verse asks you to notice when your closeness tracks someone's success.{/idea}
old: I am close to the people I care about.
new: Real care shows in the hard season, not just when there is something to share.
try: Contact one person who is going through a hard time right now, with nothing to gain from it.

title: Whoever trades this world for the next does not lose.
subtitle: Either way it ends, the reward is great
then: This verse addressed believers in Madinah during a time of armed conflict. It encouraged those {idea}who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes that whether they fell or won, {reward}they would earn an immense reward with Allah{/reward}.
now: You spend a weekend on a charity project that ends up raising almost nothing. You stood up for what was right at work and still lost the argument. {reward}The verse does not grade by the result.{/reward} What you gave up for Allah is already counted.
old: If it did not work out, my effort was for nothing.
new: When I give something up for Allah, the reward does not depend on the outcome.
try: Recall one good effort that failed. Tell Allah you did it for Him and leave the result with Him.

title: What is wrong with you, while the weak are crying out?
subtitle: The prayer of those who had no helper

key.label: The question turned on the listener

then: Some believers, men, women and children, were trapped in Makkah and could not leave. Ibn Kathir notes Ibn Abbas said, {idea}I and my mother were among the oppressed{/idea}. They prayed for Allah to {reward}send them a protector and a helper{/reward}. The verse asks the believers in Madinah why they were holding back.
now: The elderly neighbor no one checks on. The classmate everyone picks on. The relative stuck in a home where she is treated badly. {idea}They are praying for a helper.{/idea} The verse asks you directly: what is stopping you from being part of the answer?
old: Someone else will step in for people who are struggling.
new: The cry of the weak is addressed to me too, and I can be part of the answer.
try: Think of one person near you who has no one in their corner. Do one thing for them today.

title: Shaytan's plot always looks bigger than it is.
subtitle: Whose cause you are really serving

row.title: I cannot resist
sub: it is too strong for me

then: Ibn Kathir explains that believers strive {idea}in obedience to Allah and to gain His pleasure{/idea}, while others act in obedience to Shaytan. The verse encouraged the believers of Madinah and ended with a reassurance: {trap}the plot of Shaytan has always been weak{/trap}.
now: It is late and the phone is in your hand. The urge says you will never beat this habit, so why try. That is the plot talking. {idea}Allah calls it feeble.{/idea} One honest prayer and putting the phone in another room is often all it takes.
old: Some of my temptations are just too strong for me.
new: Shaytan's pull feels huge, but Allah says it is weak against someone who turns to Him.
try: Name the temptation that feels strongest, say a'udhu billah, and change rooms the next time it comes.

title: They asked for the test, then asked for more time.
subtitle: When what you wished for arrives and frightens you

row.title: the Hereafter is better
sub: no wrong, not a thread's worth

then: In Makkah, some believers were eager to defend themselves but were told to {idea}hold back, pray and give charity{/idea}. Later in Madinah, when the command came, some of them {trap}feared people as they feared Allah{/trap} and asked for a delay. The answer: this world's enjoyment is short.
now: You prayed for the job, the marriage, the move. Now it is here and it is hard, and you catch yourself asking Allah why now. {reward}The verse does not shame the fear. It puts it in proportion.{/reward} Short is this life, and nothing you do for Him is lost.
old: I wanted this, but not if it costs me this much.
new: Fear of people should not outweigh fear of Allah, and no effort for Him is wasted.
try: Write down one thing you asked Allah for that has turned out hard. Ask Him for strength in it, not escape.

title: Death finds you even in the tallest tower.
subtitle: And good and hard times both come from Allah

row.title: good is Allah, bad is them

then: Ibn Kathir quotes Khalid bin Al-Walid, wounded in many battles, saying on his deathbed: {idea}yet here I am, I die in my bed{/idea}. The verse also exposes those who credited Allah for good years but {trap}blamed the Prophet ﷺ for hard ones{/trap}.
now: Your bills are paid and you say alhamdulillah. The car breaks down and you blame your spouse for the route, your boss for the hours. {idea}Both came by Allah's decree.{/idea} And no amount of insurance or caution changes the appointed time.
old: Good things are a blessing; bad things are someone's fault.
new: Everything runs by Allah's decree, and my safety was never in towers.
try: The next time something goes wrong today, pause before blaming anyone and say inna lillah.

title: The good is His gift. Look at yourself for the rest.
subtitle: Where to look when things go wrong

row.title: what did they do to me

then: Right after saying all things are from Allah's decree, Allah addresses each person. {reward}Good is from His bounty and mercy.{/reward} Harm, said As-Suddi, Al-Hasan and others, comes {trap}because of your own errors{/trap}. A related verse adds: and He pardons much.
now: The friendship cooled. The project slipped. Your teenager stopped talking to you. Before the list of other people's faults, the verse hands you a mirror. {idea}Ask what part was yours.{/idea} Then remember He pardons much.
old: Most of what goes wrong in my life is other people's doing.
new: The good is His gift; the harm often traces back to me, and He forgives much of it.
try: Pick one recent problem and write one sentence about your own part in it. Then ask forgiveness.

title: Obeying the Messenger is obeying Allah.
subtitle: And the one who turns away carries it himself
then: Ibn Kathir explains that whatever the Messenger ﷺ says is revelation, so {idea}obeying him is obeying Allah{/idea}. To the Prophet ﷺ Allah says: you were not sent as a watcher over those who turn away. {idea}Your job is only to convey{/idea}, and they will only harm themselves.
now: You keep nagging your brother about prayer. Each argument gets louder and he drifts further. The verse frees you from a role you were never given. {idea}Share it kindly, live it well, then leave the rest.{/idea}
old: If someone I love is not practicing, I have failed unless I fix it.
new: My part is to follow the Messenger ﷺ myself and convey gently. Hearts are not mine to control.
try: Replace one reminder you would normally nag about with a quiet dua for that person.

title: Yes to your face, other plans by night.
subtitle: Allah records what is planned after the door closes
then: The hypocrites in Madinah said we obey in the Prophet's ﷺ presence, then {trap}spent the night planning the opposite{/trap}. Ibn Kathir notes Allah knew and recorded it. Yet the Prophet ﷺ was told to pardon them, not expose them, and {idea}put his trust in Allah{/idea}.
now: You say sure, sounds good in the meeting, then open a side chat to undo it. Or a parent says yes to the plan and quietly works against it. {trap}The verse sees the second conversation.{/trap} And when you are on the receiving end, it tells you: Allah is enough.
old: What I agree to in public and what I do in private are separate things.
new: Allah writes down the night plans too. If I agree, I should mean it.
try: Check today if you have said yes to something you are quietly undermining. Either commit or say no honestly.

title: Read it closely. Its own consistency is the sign.
subtitle: An invitation to think deeply about the Quran
then: Allah invites people to {idea}contemplate the Quran{/idea}, not ignore it. Ibn Kathir reports the Prophet ﷺ grew angry when Companions argued loudly over a verse, saying {trap}nations before you were ruined by setting parts of the Book against each other{/trap}. Act on what you know; refer what you do not.
now: You hear the Quran at every Ramadan taraweeh but have never sat with one page and asked what it means. Or you saw a viral clip pitting one verse against another. {idea}The invitation is to read slowly and see it hold together.{/idea}
old: I know the Quran because I have heard it many times.
new: Its truth shows when I actually think about it, and read it as one whole.
try: Read one short passage today with a translation, slowly, and write down one question it raises.

title: Before you spread it, take it to someone who knows.
subtitle: News of safety or fear, and the rush to share
then: People in Madinah would hear news about safety or danger and {trap}broadcast it before checking{/trap}. Ibn Kathir recounts Umar hearing a rumor that the Prophet ﷺ had divorced his wives. He {idea}went and asked him directly{/idea}, learned it was false, and announced it at the masjid door.
now: A forwarded voice note about a crime in your area. A screenshot about a scholar. A health scare in the family group. Your thumb is already on share. {trap}Narrating everything you hear is enough to make you a liar{/trap}, the Prophet ﷺ said. Check first.
old: I am just passing it on. If it is wrong, it is not my fault.
new: Spreading unchecked news is my responsibility. I can verify or stay quiet.
try: Before forwarding anything today, ask one question: do I know this is true? If not, do not send it.

title: You answer for yourself, even if others hang back.
subtitle: Your duty does not wait for everyone else

picture.label: The instruction to the Prophet ﷺ

row.title: if they do not, why should I
only you are asked of you

then: In a time of conflict, Allah told the Prophet ﷺ to go forward himself and {idea}not be troubled by those who stayed back{/idea}: you are only responsible for yourself. He was also told to encourage the believers. The final word: {reward}Allah is greater in might{/reward}.
now: Nobody in your house prays on time, so you drift too. Nobody on your team owns up to errors, so you stay quiet. {idea}You are asked only about yourself.{/idea} Do your part well, then encourage others gently, without waiting for them.
old: I will do better once the people around me do.
new: I answer for my own actions, and I can lead by doing them first.
try: Pick one good habit everyone around you neglects and do it yourself today, without comment.

title: Put in a word for good, and you share the reward.
subtitle: Every recommendation carries a share of its result

row.title: just a favor
sub: nothing to do with me after

then: Mujahid said this verse was about {idea}people interceding for one another{/idea}. Whoever helps bring about good gets a share of it; whoever helps bring about harm carries part of it. The Prophet ﷺ said, {reward}intercede and you will be rewarded{/reward}.
now: A friend asks you to put in a word for her with your manager. A cousin asks you to vouch for a man who wants to marry into the family. {idea}Your word has weight, and you share in what it leads to.{/idea} Use it for good and use it honestly.
old: Recommending someone is a small favor with no lasting stake for me.
new: When I speak for someone, I take a share of what comes from it.
try: Put in one good word today for someone who deserves it: a reference, a thank-you to their boss, a kind mention.

title: Return a greeting better, or at least the same.
subtitle: Even a salam is counted
