then: Ibn Kathir reports a man greeting the Prophet ﷺ with salam, and after he sat the Prophet ﷺ said {reward}ten{/reward}. The next added wa rahmatullah and he said {reward}twenty{/reward}. The verse ends: Allah is an Accountant over all things.
now: Someone says salam as you rush past in the office kitchen, and you mumble something without looking up. Someone texts a warm hello and you reply with a thumbs up. {idea}Even this is counted.{/idea} Meet warmth with a little more warmth.
old: Greetings are just politeness, not worship.
new: Returning a greeting fully and kindly is a deed Allah keeps count of.
try: Today, answer every salam with the full reply, and look the person in the eye when you say it.

title: He will gather you all. Who is truer in word?
subtitle: The certainty underneath every instruction
then: After instructions about encouraging good, interceding and greeting, Allah grounds it all: {idea}there is no god but Him{/idea}, and He will gather everyone on a Day about which {reward}there is no doubt{/reward}. And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?
now: You trust a weather app to plan your weekend and a delivery notification to plan your evening. Both get it wrong sometimes. {idea}The One who promised the Day never does.{/idea} Let that set the weight of what you do today.
old: The Day of Resurrection is real, but it does not feel close.
new: The most truthful voice says it is certain, so it can shape my ordinary choices now.
try: Before one decision today, ask yourself quietly: how will this look on the Day I am gathered?

title: Why split into two camps over them?
subtitle: When believers argue about others' hearts

row.title: guidance is Allah's
sub: they fell back by what they earned

then: Zayd bin Thabit reported that on the march to Uhud some who came along {trap}turned back to Madinah{/trap}, and the Companions split into two groups over them. Allah asked why they were divided and said these people {idea}fell back because of what they had earned{/idea}.
now: Someone in your circle has drifted, and now the group chat is two factions arguing about him. Hours of messages, and the friendships between you start to crack. {idea}His heart is between him and Allah.{/idea} Do not let it break the people still standing together.
old: If someone turns away, it is up to us to settle what they are.
new: Guidance is Allah's. Our job is not to tear each other apart over it.
try: If you are in an argument about someone else's faith, step out of it today and make dua for them instead.

title: Some want you to be just like them.
subtitle: Closeness with those who want your faith gone

row.title: trusted ally
sub: only those who help you stay true

then: This was about a specific group in wartime who claimed Islam but {trap}sided with the enemy and wanted the believers to fall away{/trap}. Ibn Kathir notes it was due to their extreme hostility. The believers were told not to take them as allies, and the following verse gave clear exceptions.
now: There is a friend who mocks you every time you skip a drink or leave to pray. A colleague who keeps saying you have changed, loosen up. {idea}Notice who wants you to be like them, and how much you lean on them.{/idea} Be kind to all; choose your close allies carefully.
old: My closest friends do not affect my faith.
new: Those who want me to drop my faith should not be the ones I lean on most.
try: Think of whose voice is loudest in your head when you hesitate to do good. Spend time today with someone who lifts you.

title: If they offer peace, there is no path against them.
subtitle: Peace and restraint built into the command

key.label: How to read a hard verse

then: Right after the previous verse, Allah excluded people tied to a peace treaty and those who {idea}had no heart to fight{/idea} either side. If they withdrew and offered peace, {idea}Allah made no way against them{/idea}. Ibn Kathir mentions Al-Abbas at Badr, who came reluctantly and was ordered spared.
now: Your sister apologizes after a big fight and asks to move on. You still have a list of points to make. {idea}When someone offers peace, the verse closes the road to more battle.{/idea} Accept it, even when part of you wants the last word.
old: Once someone has wronged me, I am free to keep pushing back.
new: When someone steps back and offers peace, my path is to accept it.
try: If someone has tried to make peace with you recently, answer it today with a warm, clear yes.

title: Safe with everyone, loyal to no one.
subtitle: Those who fall back each time they are tested

key.label: What looks the same but is not

row.title: the reluctant
sub: hearts unwilling to fight, offered peace

then: Ibn Kathir explains these people looked like the peaceful group in the previous verse, but their intention was different. They showed Islam to be safe with the believers while {trap}secretly siding with their enemies{/trap}. Every time they were tested, {trap}they fell back{/trap}. The verse dealt with them as a wartime threat.
now: You agree with whoever is in the room. Pious at the masjid, mocking at the office, neutral in the family chat. It feels safe. {idea}The verse asks what you become when you are actually tested.{/idea} Safety with everyone can mean standing for nothing.
old: Fitting in with everyone is just being easygoing.
new: If I change sides every time I am tested, I have no side.
try: Notice one place where you hide your values to fit in. Show them gently there, just once.

title: Even a harm done by mistake asks for repair.
subtitle: The weight of a life, even when unintended

row.title: I did not mean it
sub: so it is not on me

row.title: I did not mean it
sub: and I still make it right

then: The verse opens by saying a believer never kills a believer, except by mistake. Mujahid said it came about Ayyash bin Abi Rabi'ah, who killed a man he {trap}did not know had become Muslim{/trap}. Even for a mistake, Allah set out a heavy repair, to {idea}seek repentance from Allah{/idea}.
now: You reversed out of the driveway without looking and hit a neighbor's car. You forwarded a message that cost someone their job. You never meant it. {idea}The verse does not let unintended harm vanish.{/idea} It asks you to own it, repair it, and turn to Allah.
old: If I did not intend the harm, I have nothing to answer for.
new: A mistake is forgiven differently, but it still asks me to repair what I broke.
try: Think of one harm you caused without meaning to. Take one step today to make it right.

title: A believer's life is that sacred.
subtitle: The gravest warning, and what it protects

row.title: the gravest sin
sub: Allah's anger and a great punishment

then: Right after the verse on accidental killing, Allah speaks of the deliberate one. The Prophet ﷺ said {idea}the blood of a Muslim is sacred{/idea}. This verse is among the most severe warnings in the Quran, showing {trap}how grave it is to take a life{/trap}.
now: You will likely never come near this sin. But you know the heat that rises in traffic, in a shouting match, in a fight with a brother. {idea}Every harm starts as anger left unchecked.{/idea} The verse teaches you how much Allah values the person in front of you.
old: This warning is about criminals, not about me.
new: It shows how precious every believer is to Allah, and that guards how I treat people.
try: The next time anger rises today, say a'udhu billah, sit down, and stay silent for a minute.

title: He gave you salam. Do not call him a fake.
subtitle: Verify, and remember you were once hiding too
then: Ibn Abbas reported that a shepherd greeted some Companions with salam, and they said {trap}he only says it to protect himself{/trap}, killed him and took his sheep. The verse came down: verify, do not deny someone's faith for worldly gain. {idea}You were like that before{/idea}, hiding your faith in Makkah.
now: A new Muslim at your masjid says something clumsy and you whisper, she is not really practicing. Someone posts a verse and you comment, as if you pray. {idea}You cannot open their heart.{/idea} And Allah once had to be patient with you too.
old: I can tell who is sincere and who is faking.
new: I take people's faith at their word, because Allah was gentle with my beginnings too.
try: Think of someone whose faith you doubted out loud. Make a sincere dua for them today instead.

title: Not equal, except those who truly cannot.
subtitle: Effort is honored, real excuses are honored too

row.title: I cannot, so I am lesser

then: When the verse first came down, Ibn Umm Maktum, a blind Companion, said {idea}if I had the power, I would join{/idea}. Allah then added: {reward}except those who are disabled{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ later said some who stayed in Madinah were with them in every valley, held back only by their excuse.
now: You are on the sofa with an injury while your friends run the charity marathon. Or you can easily help and just do not feel like it. {idea}Those are two different seats.{/idea} Allah honors real limits, and He sees the difference.
old: Everyone who did not take part is the same.
new: Allah separates those who could not from those who would not, and both kinds of effort are seen.
try: Look at one good cause you skip. If you have a real reason, make dua for it; if not, give a little effort.

title: Ranks, forgiveness and mercy for those who strive.
subtitle: What effort for Allah opens
then: Continuing the comparison, Allah describes what He gives those who strive: {reward}degrees from Him, forgiveness and mercy{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of a hundred grades in Paradise. The verse closes with {idea}Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful{/idea}.
now: You give a little more each month, stay a little longer to help, push a little harder in your worship. It feels unnoticed. {reward}Each extra step is a degree from Him.{/reward} And the verse ends not on ranking but on forgiveness.
old: Extra effort is just extra tiredness.
new: Effort for Allah lifts me by degrees, and wraps me in His forgiveness.
try: Add one small extra to a good thing you already do, like two more rakahs or one more coin.

title: Was not Allah's earth wide enough for you?
subtitle: The question asked about staying where faith is stifled
then: Ibn Abbas said this was about some Muslims in Makkah who {trap}stayed with the idolators and even marched with their army{/trap}, though they could have left. At death the angels ask what state they were in. They claim weakness; the reply is {idea}was not Allah's earth spacious{/idea}. The warning is sober and severe.
now: A job that keeps making you compromise. A friend group that keeps pulling you away from Allah. You say, I have no choice. {idea}The verse asks you to check whether that is true.{/idea} Sometimes the door out is there, and you have not looked at it.
old: My surroundings are just how things are. I cannot change them.
new: If my surroundings are pulling me from Allah and I can move, I am asked why I stayed.
try: Name one setting that weakens your faith. Write down one realistic step that would loosen its hold.

title: Those who truly had no way out are excused.
subtitle: Allah knows the difference between can't and won't
then: Right after the warning, Allah excludes {idea}the truly weak who could not devise a plan or find a way{/idea}. Ibn Abbas said, {reward}I and my mother were among those whom Allah excused{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray in Isha for the weak believers trapped in Makkah.
now: The teenager who cannot leave a hard home. The wife with no money and no way out. The worker whose visa ties him to his boss. {reward}Allah sees exactly who cannot.{/reward} If that is you, the verse speaks with gentleness. If you know someone like that, pray for them by name.
old: Allah judges everyone by the same outward result.
new: Allah weighs what each person could actually do, and excuses the truly trapped.
try: Make dua tonight, by name, for someone you know who is stuck in a situation they cannot leave.

title: For them, expect Allah's pardon.
subtitle: Hope held out to the truly weak

key.label: What the word may means here

then: Of the weak who could not leave, Allah says {reward}it is expected that He will pardon them{/reward}. Ibn Kathir notes that here, likely {idea}means He shall{/idea}. The verse ends by naming Him the Pardoning, the Forgiving.
now: You carry guilt for years you could not pray openly, a home where you could not practice, a time you were too young or too scared to choose. {reward}Allah knows what you could not do.{/reward} Let this verse loosen that knot.
old: I should be ashamed of what I could not do back then.
new: Where I truly could not, Allah meets me with pardon.
try: Name one past situation you could not change. Tell Allah about it and ask Him to pardon you.

title: Set out for Allah, and the reward is already secured.
subtitle: The step out counts even before you arrive

row.title: leaves home
sub: for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ

row.title: room and provision
sub: a way out of what he dislikes

row.title: reward secured
sub: even if he dies on the way

then: This encouraged believers in Makkah to emigrate: they would find {reward}many places and abundance{/reward}. Ibn Kathir recalls the man who killed a hundred people, set out to repent, and died on the road. {idea}He was counted among those who had arrived{/idea}, because he was closer to the good land.
now: You have been meaning to leave a bad habit, a toxic friendship, a job that eats your prayers. You fear you will not make it all the way. {idea}The verse says the setting out is already counted.{/idea} Start walking.
old: There is no point starting if I might not finish.
new: Once I set out for Allah, the reward is His to give, whether or not I arrive.
try: Take the very first step today toward a change you have been delaying, however small.

title: An ease from Allah is a gift. Accept it.
subtitle: Lightened prayer on the road, offered with mercy

row.title: we are safe now
sub: so is it still for us?

then: In the early years after the Hijrah, most travel was dangerous. Allah lifted blame for shortening the prayer on the road. Umar later wondered why it still applied in safe times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}a charity Allah has given you, so accept His charity{/reward}.
now: You are exhausted on a long trip and feel guilty taking any ease. Or you are proud of always doing the hardest version of everything. {reward}Sometimes the humble thing is to receive what Allah gives.{/reward} His ease is love, not a lower grade.
old: Taking an ease Allah allows feels like doing less for Him.
new: Accepting His ease with gratitude is itself a way of honoring Him.
try: Next time Allah's law gives you an ease, take it and thank Him for it out loud.

title: Even facing danger, the prayer was not dropped.
subtitle: Guarding each other while standing before Allah
then: Abu Ayyash reported that at Usfan the enemy saw the Muslims at prayer and planned to strike at the next one, {trap}a prayer dearer to them than their own children{/trap}. These verses came down in between. The Prophet ﷺ led the prayer in shifts, {idea}each group guarding the other{/idea}.
now: Deadline night, a sick child, a twelve-hour shift on the ward. Your first thought is to skip the prayer. {idea}They kept it in front of an army.{/idea} And they did it by covering for each other. Who could you cover for so they can pray?
old: When life gets intense, prayer is the first thing to go.
new: Prayer stays, even in the hardest moments; we just help each other keep it.
try: At your busiest point today, take five minutes to pray on time, or cover for someone so they can.

title: Standing, sitting, lying down, keep remembering Him.
subtitle: Prayer has its times; remembrance has none
then: After the prayer in fear, Allah tells the believers to {idea}remember Him standing, sitting and lying down{/idea}, in every condition. When safe, they should pray fully and humbly. Ibn Abbas said prayer has {reward}a fixed time, just as Hajj does{/reward}.
now: You fold the prayer mat and pick up your phone, and Allah is out of your mind until the next adhan. The bus ride, the queue, the moment before sleep are all empty. {idea}The verse fills those gaps.{/idea} A quiet subhanallah fits in any posture.
old: I remember Allah when I pray.
new: Prayer is at its times, and remembrance fills everything in between.
try: Pick one daily wait, like the bus or the kettle, and make it your moment for dhikr today.

title: They hurt like you hurt. But you have hope.
subtitle: Same pain, different horizon
then: After battle the believers were wounded and tired. Allah told them not to weaken: {idea}they suffer as you suffer{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes the difference is that {reward}you hope from Allah for reward and help{/reward}, while they do not.
now: You are worn out from a long illness, a hard degree, a marriage you are working to save. Everyone struggles; you are not uniquely weak. {reward}What you carry that others may not is hope in Allah.{/reward} Let that be the thing that keeps you going.
old: I am struggling more than anyone, so maybe I should give up.
new: Everyone hurts, but I have hope in Allah, and that is reason enough to keep going.
try: When you feel like quitting today, say one dua that names what you are hoping Allah will give.

title: Do not become the advocate of the dishonest.
subtitle: Judging by truth, not by who argues best

row.conn: but if it is not his right

then: Allah sent the Book {idea}in truth, to judge by what Allah has shown{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ warned that he was only human and judged by what he heard: if someone won a case unfairly, {trap}it was a piece of the Fire{/trap}. Two disputing men wept and each gave up his claim.
now: Your cousin is in a dispute with a neighbor and the family expects you to back him. You know he is in the wrong. {trap}Arguing well for him does not make it right.{/trap} The verse asks you not to be the lawyer for something false.
old: Loyalty means always taking my people's side.
new: Loyalty never means defending what I know is dishonest.
try: If you are backing someone in an argument, ask yourself honestly whether they are in the right. Act on the answer.

title: After a call on justice, ask forgiveness.
subtitle: Turning to Allah after weighing others

row.title: I ask forgiveness
sub: for what I may have missed

then: Right after warning against siding with the deceitful, Allah says simply: {idea}seek forgiveness of Allah{/idea}. The command sits between instructions about judging fairly, a reminder that {reward}Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful{/reward}.
now: You mediated a fight between two friends and picked a side. You made a call at work that hurt someone's bonus. Even if you did your best, there may be things you missed. {idea}A quiet astaghfirullah after a hard call keeps you humble.{/idea}
old: If I tried to be fair, there is nothing to seek forgiveness for.
new: After any judgment on others, I turn to Allah for what I may have missed.
try: After the next decision you make about someone else today, say astaghfirullah three times.

title: Do not argue for those who betray themselves.
subtitle: Defending a deceiver hurts more than him
then: Continuing the passage, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ {idea}not to argue on behalf of those who deceive themselves{/idea}. Their deceit is against their own souls. And Allah does not love {trap}one who is a habitual, sinful betrayer{/trap}.
now: A colleague asks you to tell the manager he was with you all afternoon. A friend asks you to back up her story to her husband. {trap}Covering for deceit drags you into it.{/trap} You can stay kind without lending your voice.
old: Covering for a friend is a small kindness.
new: Arguing for someone's deceit harms them, harms me, and is not loved by Allah.
try: If someone asks you to back up a story that is not true, decline gently today and say why.

title: Hidden from people, never hidden from Allah.
subtitle: He is with them when they plot at night

row.title: no one will know
sub: as long as people do not

then: Ibn Kathir explains that they {trap}hid their wrongdoing from people so as not to be criticized{/trap}, yet exposed it to Allah, who knows their secrets. He is {idea}with them by His knowledge{/idea} when they spend the night in talk He does not accept.
now: You clear your browser history. You delete the message thread. You make sure your parents never find out. {idea}You worked so hard to hide it from people and forgot the One who was there.{/idea} He is also the One who forgives.
old: As long as nobody finds out, it is manageable.
new: I hide things from people but not from Allah, so He is the One I should face.
try: Think of one thing you hide from people. Tonight, talk to Allah about it honestly.

title: You defended them here. Who will defend them there?
subtitle: A verdict here is not a verdict there
then: Ibn Kathir explains that people might win a ruling in this world, since judges see only what is apparent. {trap}But on the Day of Resurrection, who will argue for them before Allah{/trap}, who knows the secret and what is more hidden? {idea}No one will speak for them.{/idea}
now: You got the refund you did not deserve. You won the family argument with a clever spin. Your lawyer got the better share of the inheritance. {idea}This is a reminder that the case is not closed.{/idea} There is still time to make it right.
old: If I won it fairly by the rules, it is mine.
new: Winning here does not settle anything before Allah, who knows what really happened.
try: Think of one thing you won that you were not entitled to. Take one step to give it back.

title: Whatever you did, ask, and you will find Him forgiving.
subtitle: The door stays open after any wrong
then: After the warnings to the deceitful, Allah opens the door wide. Ibn Abbas said whoever sins, minor or major, then asks forgiveness, will find Allah forgiving {reward}even if his sins were greater than the heavens, the earth and the mountains{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of {idea}wudu, two rakahs and asking forgiveness{/idea}.
now: It is two in the morning and you are lying awake over something you did years ago. You assume it is too late. {reward}The verse says: ask, and you will find Him.{/reward} Get up, make wudu, pray two rakahs, and tell Him.
old: What I did is too big to be forgiven.
new: No sin is bigger than Allah's forgiveness when I sincerely ask.
try: Tonight, make wudu, pray two rakahs, and ask Allah to forgive one specific thing.

title: Every sin you earn lands on your own account.
subtitle: No one else carries your burden
then: Right after promising forgiveness to anyone who asks, Allah adds: {trap}whoever earns a sin earns it against himself{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse that no bearer of burdens carries another's burden. It flows from Allah's {idea}knowledge, wisdom, fairness and mercy{/idea}.
now: You blame the group chat for the gossip you joined. You blame your upbringing for the temper you never worked on. {idea}Those influences are real, but the sin you choose is yours.{/idea} The good news: so is the repentance.
old: Part of what I did wrong belongs to the people who pushed me.
new: What I choose is mine to answer for, and mine to repent from.
try: Say one wrong you did today out loud, starting with I, not with anyone else's name.

title: Blaming the innocent doubles the sin.
subtitle: The slander that makes your own wrong heavier
then: Ibn Kathir titles this passage a {trap}warning to those who falsely accuse innocent people{/trap}. Whoever commits a fault and blames it on someone innocent {trap}has burdened himself with slander and a clear sin{/trap}, on top of what he did.
now: The vase is broken and you say your little brother did it. The report was late and you say the intern dropped the ball. {trap}Now you carry two sins and someone else carries your shame.{/trap} The verse asks you to stop at one.
old: Letting someone else take the blame is just self-protection.
new: Blaming an innocent adds slander to my sin and wrongs another person.
try: If someone took blame for something you did, tell them, or the person who blamed them, today.

title: Allah's favor kept him from being misled.
subtitle: Taught what he did not know
then: Some people tried to steer the Prophet ﷺ into a wrong judgment, but {trap}they misled only themselves{/trap}. Allah reminds him: He sent down the Book and wisdom and {reward}taught you what you did not know{/reward}. Ibn Kathir links this to the verse that he did not know what the Book was before.
now: Someone is working hard to pull you into a scheme, a lie, a fight that is not yours. Your protection is not cleverness. {reward}It is what Allah has taught you, kept close.{/reward} The ayat you know are a shield you may not notice you are holding.
old: I avoid being misled because I am sharp.
new: What keeps me straight is what Allah has taught me, and that is His favor.
try: Thank Allah today for one thing in the Quran that has kept you from a mistake.

title: Most whispers are empty, except these three.
subtitle: Private talk that is worth having

picture.label: The good kind of secret talk

row.title: mending relations
sub: the Prophet ﷺ ranked it higher

then: Allah says there is no good in most private talk, {idea}except urging charity, good, or reconciliation{/idea}. Abu Ad-Darda' reported the Prophet ﷺ said mending relations between people is better than the grade of extra fasting, prayer and charity, and that {trap}spoiling relations is the destroyer{/trap}.
now: Look at your direct messages from this week. How much was complaint, gossip, or plans that go nowhere? {reward}Now imagine one message that helps two estranged cousins talk again.{/reward} That is the kind of whisper the verse rewards.
old: What I say in private does not really matter.
new: Private talk is either empty or it is charity, good counsel and peacemaking.
try: Send one private message today that encourages charity, gives good advice, or helps two people reconcile.

title: Turn away after seeing clearly, and you get what you chose.
subtitle: Allah leaves a person on the path they pick
then: This is about someone who opposes the Messenger ﷺ {trap}after guidance has become clear{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {trap}makes the chosen path look good to him{/trap}, so he goes further, as in the verse: when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away. The warning is sober.
now: You know the habit is wrong. At first you feel guilty every time. After a year, you have reasons for it. After two, you defend it. {idea}That slow shift is what the verse warns about.{/idea} The sooner you turn back, the easier it is.
old: I will deal with this when I am ready; it will stay the same until then.
new: Staying on a path I know is wrong changes how it looks to me, so I turn back now.
try: Name one wrong you have started to justify. Write down the reason you first knew it was wrong.

title: Everything but shirk can be forgiven.
subtitle: The one line Allah draws, and the wide mercy below it
then: Allah repeats a line from earlier in the surah: {trap}He does not forgive associating partners with Him{/trap}, but {reward}forgives what is less than that for whom He wills{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says whoever associates partners strays far and loses contentment in both lives.
now: You worry endlessly about small sins but never think about where your heart actually leans. Luck charms, fear of what people think, money as your real safety. {idea}Guard your tawhid most of all.{/idea} Below that line, Allah's mercy is wide.
old: My biggest risk is the number of my sins.
new: My biggest care is keeping my worship for Allah alone, and hoping in His mercy for the rest.
try: Ask yourself honestly: what do I rely on as if it were Allah? Say la ilaha illallah with that in mind.

title: Behind every false god, the one really obeyed is Shaytan.
subtitle: Who is actually being served

picture.label: What they thought vs what it was

then: Ad-Dahhak said the idolators claimed the angels were Allah's daughters and {trap}carved idols shaped like girls to worship them{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains that Shaytan ordered this and made it look beautiful, so {trap}in reality they were worshipping Shaytan{/trap}.
now: You do not bow to statues. But when you check your phone before your prayer, or bend your values for a promotion, ask who is giving the orders. {idea}The thing itself is not the master; the voice behind it is.{/idea}
old: I would never worship anything other than Allah.
new: Whatever I obey over Allah, I am really obeying the one who whispered it.
try: Notice one thing today that you obeyed before Allah. Ask who was really behind that pull.

title: Shaytan announced his plan: a share of Allah's servants.
subtitle: The enemy who told you exactly what he wants
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {trap}expelled Shaytan and banished him from His mercy{/trap}. Shaytan then vowed to take {trap}a fixed and known share{/trap} of Allah's servants. He is an enemy who has openly declared what he is after.
now: If a stranger told you he was going to steal from your house, you would lock the doors. Shaytan said it plainly and you still leave the door open: the late nights, the endless scroll, the anger you never check. {idea}He told you his plan. Act like you heard it.{/idea}
old: Shaytan is mostly a concern for people worse than me.
new: He openly wants a share of all of Allah's servants, so I guard myself.
try: Close one door Shaytan uses with you, like an app, a habit, or a time of night, for one day.

title: His tools: misleading, false hopes, and tampering with creation.
subtitle: How Shaytan works, in his own words
then: Shaytan lists his methods. Ibn Kathir explains the false hopes as {trap}encouraging people to delay and procrastinate with good deeds{/trap}. He would also command invented rituals like slitting the ears of cattle, and changing Allah's creation. Whoever takes him as an ally {trap}suffers a clear loss{/trap}.
now: I will start praying properly after exams. I will give charity once I get the raise. I will make up with my father next Eid. {trap}Each one sounds like a plan. It is a false hope.{/trap} The verse names procrastination as one of his tools.
old: Putting off good deeds a little is harmless.
new: The comfortable someday is one of Shaytan's tools. Today is what I have.
try: Pick one good deed you keep saying you will start soon. Do it today, even in a small form.

title: His promises are only delusion.
subtitle: What Shaytan offers, and what it turns out to be

row.title: Shaytan's
sub: I betrayed you, he will admit

then: Ibn Kathir explains that Shaytan {trap}deceitfully promises his followers that they will win in this life and the next{/trap}. He cites the verse where, once all is decided, Shaytan admits: {idea}Allah promised you the truth, and I promised you and betrayed you{/idea}.
now: One more scroll will relax you. One small lie will fix it. The purchase will finally make you happy. You have heard these promises before, and you know how each one ended. {idea}Notice the pattern: the promise never delivers.{/idea}
old: This time the shortcut will actually give me what I want.
new: Shaytan's promises always end empty; only Allah's promise is true.
try: Next time a temptation promises you something, say out loud: that is a delusion. Then walk away.

title: The promises that felt so sweet lead nowhere safe.
subtitle: Where Shaytan's promises end
then: The verses before this describe Shaytan's plan: mislead people, stir up {trap}false hopes{/trap}, and push them to delay good deeds. Ibn Kathir explains that this verse names the end of those who prefer what he promises. On the Day, Shaytan himself will admit he betrayed them.
now: You tell yourself you will pray properly once things calm down. You will fix that habit after the exams, after the wedding, after the promotion. {trap}Later keeps moving.{/trap} The verse is sober so that you stop trusting the voice that says later, and {idea}turn now while turning is easy.{/idea}
old: There is always time to sort myself out later.
new: The voice selling me later is the one that never keeps its word.
try: Pick one good thing you keep postponing and do the smallest piece of it today.

title: One promise is true, and it comes from Allah.
subtitle: Two promises set side by side
then: Right after the verse about Shaytan's empty promises comes this one. Ibn Kathir says it describes believers whose {idea}hearts were truthful and whose limbs obeyed.{/idea} The verse ends with a question: {reward}who is more truthful than Allah?{/reward}
now: You have been let down. A friend who said they would be there. An employer who promised a raise. A plan that collapsed. It is easy to stop trusting any promise. {idea}This one is different.{/idea} It does not depend on anyone's mood or budget.
old: Promises get broken, so I stop counting on any of them.
new: People break promises, but Allah's promise is the one I can lean my whole weight on.
try: Do one good deed today purely because you trust Allah's promise, and tell no one.

title: Wishing does not get you there. Deeds do.
subtitle: Wishful thinking versus what you actually do

row.title: my label saves me
sub: I belong to the right side

then: Qatadah reported that believers and People of the Scripture were boasting to each other about whose prophet and book were better. The verse cut through {trap}both sides' wishful thinking.{/trap} Aishah called it one of the hardest verses, and the Prophet ﷺ comforted the companions: {reward}even a thorn's prick that hurts a believer wipes away sin.{/reward}
now: You win the argument in the comment section about whose group is better. Then you close the app and snap at your mother. {trap}Belonging is not the same as doing.{/trap} The verse turns the question from who you are with to {idea}what you actually did today.{/idea}
old: I am on the right side, so I am fine.
new: Being on the right side only counts if my actions show it.
try: Skip one argument about whose side is better today and do one quiet good deed instead.

title: Not even a speck on a date seed is lost.
subtitle: Good deeds from men and women, fully counted

row.title: a naqir
sub: a speck on a date seed

then: After warning that evil is repaid, the verse shows the other side. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah accepts good deeds {idea}from men and women alike{/idea}, with faith as the condition. The naqir is the {reward}tiny speck on the back of a date seed.{/reward} Even that much will not be withheld.
now: The dishes you washed that nobody thanked you for. The night shift no one sees. The care you give an elderly parent while your siblings are busy. {trap}It feels invisible.{/trap} {reward}None of it is lost.{/reward}
old: If nobody saw it, it probably did not count.
new: Allah counts what nobody else saw, down to the smallest speck.
try: Do one small kind thing today that no one will ever know about.

title: Hand your whole self to Allah, and do it well.
subtitle: The two conditions of a good deed
then: This verse answers the boasting in the verses before it. Ibn Kathir explains that a deed needs {idea}two things: sincerity and correctness.{/idea} Done for Allah alone, and done the way He taught. The verse points to Ibrahim, whom {reward}Allah took as an intimate friend.{/reward}
now: You post the charity receipt. You pray faster when someone is watching. Or you do something your own way and call it good because you meant well. {trap}Half a deed.{/trap} The verse asks for {idea}a whole heart and a right method{/idea}, the way Ibrahim gave his.
old: As long as I mean well, how I do it does not matter.
new: A good deed is sincere inside and done right outside.
try: Before one act of worship today, pause and say quietly: this is only for You.

title: Everything belongs to Him, and nothing escapes His knowledge.
subtitle: Ownership and awareness that surround everything

row.title: His, on loan
sub: and He sees all of it

then: This verse closes a passage about deeds, sincerity, and Ibrahim's friendship with Allah. After calling people to hand themselves over to Allah, it reminds them {idea}whose world they live in.{/idea} He owns everything and {reward}His knowledge surrounds every thing.{/reward}
now: You look at your bank app, your car keys, the house you finally bought. {trap}It all feels like mine.{/trap} Then you hear of someone who lost everything in a week. {idea}It was always on loan{/idea}, and the Owner sees how you use it.
old: What I have earned is simply mine.
new: What I hold is His, and He sees how I handle it.
try: Pick one thing you own and use it today to help someone else.

title: The weakest in your care are the ones Allah watches over.
subtitle: Orphan girls and children who had no voice
then: People asked the Prophet ﷺ about women, and Allah answered. Aishah explained that some guardians held an orphan girl's wealth with their own. {trap}They would marry her for her money, or block her from marrying anyone else.{/trap} Ibn Abbas said young children were also denied inheritance. The verse called for {idea}justice to orphans.{/idea}
now: You are the older sibling handling the family money after a parent dies. Or the relative quietly managing a widow's paperwork. {trap}No one checks the numbers.{/trap} The verse says {idea}Allah knows every good you do{/idea} for the one who cannot speak up.
old: If no one checks, small advantages for me are fine.
new: The person who cannot defend themselves has Allah defending them.
try: Think of someone who depends on you. Do one thing today that protects their interest over yours.

title: Making peace is better, even when it costs you something.
subtitle: When a marriage drifts and greed pulls both ways

row.title: the soul's grip
sub: I will not give an inch

then: Ibn Kathir notes that Sawdah, a wife of the Prophet ﷺ, feared being divorced as she grew older. She offered her day to Aishah, and he kept her as his wife. The verse says {idea}reconciliation is better{/idea}, and admits that {trap}souls are prone to stinginess.{/trap}
now: You and your spouse have gone quiet for weeks. Each of you is waiting for the other to apologise first. {trap}Keeping score feels like protecting yourself.{/trap} The verse is honest: everyone clutches. And then it says {idea}peace is better{/idea}, and Allah sees the good you do.
old: If I give a little, I lose.
new: Letting go of a little to keep peace is a gain Allah sees.
try: Make the first small move toward someone you have gone cold with: one kind message.

title: You cannot control your heart, but do not leave anyone hanging.
subtitle: Fairness where feelings cannot be equal
then: The verse admits that a husband will never be perfectly equal between wives, even if he tries. The Prophet ﷺ shared his time equally and prayed: {idea}this is my division in what I own, so do not blame me for what You own.{/idea} He meant the heart. The warning is to not {trap}leave one neither married nor free.{/trap}
now: You feel closer to one person than another in your home, and you cannot switch that off. {trap}But one of them is sitting by the phone, waiting for a call that never comes.{/trap} The verse does not ask for equal feelings. It asks you {idea}not to leave anyone hanging.{/idea}
old: Since I cannot feel the same for everyone, fairness is impossible.
new: I owe fairness in what I control and mercy where I fall short.
try: Think of the person in your life you give the least attention. Give them ten real minutes today.

title: Even when it ends, Allah's abundance is enough for both.
subtitle: Hope after a separation
then: Ibn Kathir describes three situations in these verses: a husband drifting, a husband preferring one wife, and a couple who part. For the last, the promise is that {reward}Allah will enrich each of them{/reward} from His bounty. He is {idea}vast in giving and wise in what He decides.{/idea}
now: The relatives whisper after your divorce. You sit in the car outside your empty flat, sure your future is gone. {trap}It feels like the end of you.{/trap} The verse says the door you closed is not the only door. {reward}Allah's provision is wide enough for both of you.{/reward}
old: After this ending, there is nothing good left for me.
new: An ending is not the edge of Allah's provision.
try: Write down one thing you still have after a loss, and thank Allah for it by name.

title: The same advice for every generation: be mindful of Allah.
subtitle: One instruction given to all, and a Lord who needs no one

row.title: Allah needs my worship
sub: I am doing Him a favor

row.title: Free of need
sub: I am the one who gains

then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah gave {idea}the same instruction{/idea} to the People of the Scripture before and to the believers: be mindful of Him and worship Him alone. If people refuse, everything in the heavens and earth is still His. He is {reward}free of need and worthy of all praise.{/reward}
now: You pray and somewhere inside a small voice says you have done Allah a favor today. {trap}As if He was waiting on you.{/trap} The verse turns it around. The whole universe is His. {idea}The prayer is for you{/idea}, like water is for the thirsty.
old: My worship is something I give to Allah.
new: My worship is something Allah gives to me, because He needs nothing.
try: Before your next prayer, thank Allah for letting you stand before Him.

title: He owns it all, and He is enough to trust with it.
subtitle: Allah as the One who manages your affairs
then: This is the second time in a short space that the verse says everything belongs to Allah. Ibn Kathir explains that He {idea}watches over every soul{/idea}, knows what it deserves, and witnesses all things. {reward}He is enough as the One who handles affairs.{/reward}
now: It is two in the morning and you are lying awake running numbers. The rent, the school fees, your father's medication. {trap}It feels like everything holds together only if you never stop.{/trap} Do your part, then put it down. {reward}Allah is enough to carry the rest.{/reward}
old: If I do not hold everything together, it will all collapse.
new: I do my part and leave the outcome with the One who owns it all.
try: Tonight before sleep, name your biggest worry and say: Allah is enough for me.

title: Nobody is irreplaceable to Allah. Your place is a gift.
subtitle: He can bring others in your place
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah can {trap}take people away and replace them{/trap} if they disobey Him. He links it to another verse: if you turn away, He will bring a people unlike you. Being part of His work is {idea}an honor, not an entitlement.{/idea}
now: You run the youth circle at the mosque. You started the charity drive. {trap}Some days you think it would all stop without you.{/trap} The verse is a gentle shake. {idea}Allah's work goes on with or without you.{/idea} Being used for it is the gift.
old: This good work would fall apart without me.
new: It is a gift that Allah lets me be part of His work at all.
try: Thank Allah today for one role you have in doing good, and do it humbly.

title: Want this world? Its reward and the next are both with Allah.
subtitle: Why settle for half the reward
then: Ibn Kathir addresses this to those whose ultimate desire is this life: {idea}Allah owns the reward of both worlds.{/idea} If you ask Him for both, He will enrich you. He points to the prayer for {reward}good in this world and good in the Hereafter.{/reward}
now: You are chasing the raise, the bigger flat, the new car. Nothing wrong with wanting them. {trap}But if that is all you ask for, you have asked too small.{/trap} The One who gives the raise also holds what lasts. {reward}Ask Him for both.{/reward}
old: I will focus on this life now and think about the next one later.
new: The same Lord holds both rewards, so I ask Him for both together.
try: Next time you make dua for something worldly, add a request for the Hereafter alongside it.

title: Stand for justice, even when it costs you or your family.
subtitle: Honest testimony that does not bend for anyone
then: Ibn Kathir explains that believers are to stand for justice and {idea}not fear anyone's blame{/idea} in doing so. Testimony should be exact, even if it harms you or your parents. Do not favor the rich or pity the poor, because Allah protects both. The verse warns against {trap}twisting your words or hiding the truth.{/trap}
now: Your brother scraped another car in the car park and asks you to say you saw nothing. Your manager wants you to keep quiet about a mistake that cost a colleague their job. {trap}Loyalty says bend.{/trap} The verse says {idea}the truth stands above everyone{/idea}, even the people you love.
old: Family comes first, even before the truth.
new: I serve my family best by not lying for them.
try: Notice one moment today where you are tempted to shade the truth for someone. Say it straight, kindly.

title: You believe already. Now believe again, and keep believing.
subtitle: Faith that is renewed, not just held
then: The verse calls people who already believe to believe. Ibn Kathir says this is {idea}not repetition but completion{/idea}: keeping faith alive and whole. He compares it to the believer asking in every prayer, {reward}guide us to the straight path{/reward}, which means keep us on it and increase us.
now: You said the shahada years ago, or were born into it. Since then it has sat in the background like an app you never open. {trap}Faith can go stale without anyone noticing.{/trap} The verse asks you to {idea}renew it, today, on purpose.{/idea}
old: I am already a believer, so this verse is not for me.
new: Belief is something I keep feeding, or it quietly fades.
try: In your next prayer, say guide us to the straight path slowly and mean it as a fresh request.

title: In and out, in and out, until the door stays shut.
subtitle: The danger of a faith that keeps switching
then: Ibn Kathir explains this as someone who enters faith, leaves, enters, leaves, then {trap}stays in disbelief and grows in it until death.{/trap} Ibn Abbas said it means they remain that way until they die. The verse describes {idea}where that pattern ends{/idea}, not a door closed on the living who turn back.
now: Ramadan you are in the front row. By Shawwal you have stopped praying. Next year the same again. {trap}Each time it gets a little easier to drift.{/trap} The verse is a warning about {idea}the direction of the pattern.{/idea} Break it while you still can.
old: I can drift for a while and always come back.
new: Every drift makes the next one easier, so I hold on now.
try: Pick one act of worship you dropped after a high season and restart its smallest version today.

title: The news for a two-faced heart is not good news.
subtitle: A warning about hypocrisy

row.title: tidings
sub: the word used for good news

then: Ibn Kathir links this to the verse before: hypocrites {trap}believe, then disbelieve{/trap}, and their hearts become sealed. They show loyalty to the believers in public and to the other side in private. The verse uses the word for good tidings, but {idea}the news is a warning.{/idea}
now: You are one person at the family dinner and a different one with your friends on Friday night. {trap}Each crowd hears what it wants.{/trap} The verse is not for pointing at others. It is a mirror: {idea}am I the same person in every room?{/idea}
old: Everyone acts a bit differently around different people.
new: There is a line between adjusting my tone and splitting my loyalty, and I watch it.
try: Think of one place where you hide your faith to fit in. Show one small sign of it there today.

title: Looking for honor in the wrong crowd? All honor is Allah's.
subtitle: Where real dignity comes from
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites gave their loyalty in secret to those opposing the believers, {trap}hoping to gain honor and strength{/trap} from them. The verse asks: is that where you look for it? {reward}All honor belongs to Allah{/reward}, and He gives it to His faithful servants.
now: You laugh at a joke about your faith because the popular people at work are laughing. You drop your values to get into the right circle. {trap}It feels like moving up.{/trap} The verse says {reward}the honor you are chasing is not theirs to give.{/reward}
old: Being accepted by the important people will give me worth.
new: My worth comes from Allah, and no crowd can give or take it.
try: Notice one moment today where you trade your values for approval. Hold your ground gently.

title: When they mock Allah's words, do not stay seated.
subtitle: Staying silent in the room is a choice too
then: The verse refers back to an earlier instruction revealed in Makkah. Ibn Kathir explains that whoever {trap}stays and approves while Allah's verses are mocked{/trap} shares in what is being done. The instruction is simple: {idea}leave until they change the subject.{/idea}
now: The group chat starts making fun of the Quran. Everyone sends laughing faces. {trap}You do not join in, but you do not leave either.{/trap} The verse says the quiet seat is not neutral. {idea}Step out, or change the subject.{/idea}
old: As long as I am not the one mocking, I am fine.
new: Staying comfortable while my faith is mocked is a choice I am making.
try: Next time a conversation mocks what you hold sacred, change the subject or quietly step away.

title: Friends only when you are winning are watching, not standing with you.
subtitle: The fence-sitter who switches sides with the score

row.title: Allah judges
sub: hearts laid open on the Day

then: Ibn Kathir says the hypocrites {trap}watched and waited{/trap} to see what would happen to the believers. When the believers won, they claimed to be with them. When the other side had a success, as at Uhud, they claimed credit there. The verse says {idea}Allah will judge between them on the Day{/idea}, when the secrets of hearts come out.
now: At work there is a dispute between two managers. You agree with whoever is in the room. {trap}You wait to see who wins before saying what you believe.{/trap} It feels smart and safe. The verse says one Judge sees {idea}which side you were really on.{/idea}
old: Staying neutral until I know who wins is just being careful.
new: Allah sees whether I stand for the truth or just for the winner.
try: Say one honest thing today you have been holding back until you knew which way the wind blew.

title: A prayer for the audience, dragged and empty of remembrance.
subtitle: Lazy prayer and the eyes of people
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah can never be deceived, since He knows {idea}what hearts conceal.{/idea} The hypocrites stood for prayer {trap}lazily, to be seen, remembering Allah only a little.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ said the heaviest prayers for them were Isha and Fajr, and that if people knew their reward, {reward}they would come even crawling.{/reward}
now: You pray properly at the mosque on Friday when your uncle is next to you. At home, alone, you rush through Isha with the TV on. {trap}Fajr is the one you skip most.{/trap} The verse is a mirror, not a label. {idea}Who is your prayer really for?{/idea}
old: As long as I pray, how I feel inside does not matter much.
new: The prayer nobody sees is the truest test of who I pray for.
try: Pray your next prayer alone as slowly as you would if someone you respect were watching.

title: Swaying between two flocks, belonging to neither.
subtitle: The cost of never choosing

key.label: What sitting on the fence gives you

then: Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites were {trap}with the believers outwardly and with the other side inwardly{/trap}, swaying with every doubt. The Prophet ﷺ compared such a person to {idea}a sheep wandering between two flocks{/idea}, going to one, then the other, unsure whom to follow.
now: One week you are serious about your deen. The next you are mocking it with your old friends. {trap}You keep both doors half open.{/trap} You end up feeling at home in neither. The verse asks you to {idea}pick a flock and walk with it.{/idea}
old: Keeping a foot in both worlds means I lose nothing.
new: Never choosing means I belong nowhere, and peace comes from committing.
try: Make one clear choice today about a habit you keep going back and forth on.

title: Do not hand Allah a clear case against yourself.
subtitle: Whose side you choose to stand on
then: Revealed while the young Madinan community faced open hostility. Ibn Kathir explains the warning as against {trap}taking the opposing side as close allies{/trap} instead of the believers, giving them counsel and exposing the believers' secrets. Ibn Abbas said sultan here means {idea}proof.{/idea}
now: Your choices leave a record. The friends you lean on, whose advice shapes you, who you defend when it costs you. {trap}Every small betrayal of your own values adds a line.{/trap} The verse asks: {idea}are you building a case for yourself, or against yourself?{/idea}
old: Where my loyalties lie is a small, private matter.
new: My loyalties are evidence, and I am the one writing it.
try: Think of one person whose advice pulls you away from your values. Ask someone wiser instead this week.

title: The two-faced heart sinks lowest, with no one to help.
subtitle: Why hypocrisy is so serious
then: Ibn Kathir notes that scholars said the Fire has {trap}lower and lower depths{/trap}, just as Paradise has higher and higher grades. The hypocrites will be at the bottom, with no one to save them. The very next verse opens {idea}a way out through repentance.{/idea}
now: This is a hard verse, and it is meant to be. You do not read it to place anyone else. You read it to check {idea}whether your faith is the same inside and out.{/idea} If it is not, the next verse is waiting for you.
old: Hypocrisy is about other people, not me.
new: I check my own heart for a split before I worry about anyone else's.
try: Ask Allah tonight: make my inside better than my outside.

title: Even from the lowest point, four steps lead back.
subtitle: The way out for the one who split their heart
then: Right after the warning about the lowest depth, Allah makes an exception. Ibn Kathir explains that whoever among them {idea}repents sincerely, does good, relies on Allah, and replaces showing off with sincerity{/idea}, Allah accepts. Then {reward}they will be with the believers{/reward}, and even small deeds will benefit them.
now: You have been fake for years. Praying for show, saying what people wanted, believing half of it. {trap}You think it is too late to be real.{/trap} The verse gives four steps and no deadline. {reward}Start with the first one today.{/reward}
old: After pretending so long, I cannot become sincere now.
new: The moment I turn sincerely, I am counted with the believers.
try: Do one act of worship today that no one could ever see, purely for Allah.

title: What would Allah gain by punishing you if you are grateful?
subtitle: A Lord who appreciates
then: After the strong warnings about hypocrisy, this verse softens everything. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is {idea}too rich to need anyone{/idea}, and punishes only because of sin. He is {reward}Shakir: He appreciates those who appreciate Him{/reward}, and knows whose hearts believe.
now: You picture Allah like a strict teacher, red pen ready. {trap}Every mistake you make feels like proof He is angry.{/trap} The verse asks a gentle question. Why would He punish someone who thanks Him and believes? {reward}He is the One who notices your effort.{/reward}
old: Allah is just waiting for me to mess up.
new: Allah is the Appreciative, and He sees every grateful effort.
try: Thank Allah out loud for three specific things before you sleep tonight.

title: Allah does not love loud ugly words, except from the wronged.
subtitle: Speaking out when you have been hurt
then: Ibn Abbas explained that Allah allows the {idea}wronged person to call on Him against the one who wronged them{/idea}, though patience is better. Al-Hasan advised praying, help me against him and take my right from him. Another scholar said: if someone lies about you, {trap}you may not lie about them.{/trap}
now: Your colleague took credit for your project in front of the whole team. You are furious and the reply is already typed. {trap}It is full of insults and a few exaggerations.{/trap} The verse lets you name the wrong. It does not let you {idea}become a wrongdoer in return.{/idea}
old: Once someone wrongs me, I can say whatever I like about them.
new: I may speak of the wrong done to me, but I do not cross into wronging back.
try: If someone has hurt you, make this dua: O Allah, help me and give me my right.

title: Show good, hide good, or pardon. Allah pardons while able.
subtitle: The higher road after being wronged
then: Right after permitting the wronged to speak, the verse points higher. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}forgiving those who wrong you brings you closer to Allah.{/idea} Allah pardons even though He is fully able to punish. A hadith says {reward}Allah only increases the honor of one who pardons.{/reward}
now: Your sister said something cruel at the family dinner a year ago. You have every right to stay angry. {trap}Holding it feels like strength.{/trap} The verse offers another kind: {reward}letting go while you could hit back.{/reward} That is how Allah treats you.
old: If I forgive, I am letting them off and looking weak.
new: Pardoning when I could retaliate is strength, and Allah raises me for it.
try: Pick one old hurt and say quietly: for Allah's sake, I let this go.

title: Guidance cannot be split into parts you like and parts you skip.
subtitle: Picking and choosing among Allah's messengers
then: The verse describes people who {trap}accepted some of Allah's messengers and rejected others.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains that they followed desire and inherited habit, with no proof for the distinction. Rejecting one messenger out of envy or bias shows that {idea}the faith was never about the message{/idea} in the first place.
now: You love the verses about mercy and skip the ones about honesty in business. You quote the hadith that suits your argument and ignore the one that does not. {trap}A faith built from your preferences.{/trap} The verse asks you to {idea}take guidance whole, not as a menu.{/idea}
old: I take the parts of the deen that fit my life.
new: If I only accept what suits me, I am following myself, not guidance.
try: Find one teaching you have quietly been skipping and take one small step toward it.

title: Half-belief chosen by preference is not belief at all.
subtitle: Why picking and choosing is named so plainly
then: This continues the verse before it about believing in some messengers and rejecting others. Ibn Kathir explains that if their belief in one messenger were real, {idea}they would have accepted the others too{/idea}, or at least searched for the truth about them. Rejecting by whim shows {trap}the faith was following desire, not proof.{/trap}
now: You say you follow the truth. Then someone shows you clear evidence on a point you did not like, and you change the subject. {trap}Your faith stops exactly where your comfort stops.{/trap} The verse asks for {idea}a heart that follows proof even when it costs you.{/idea}
old: Believing most of it is close enough.
new: If I only accept truth when it suits me, I am really following myself.
try: Think of one truth you have resisted because it was inconvenient. Sit with it honestly for five minutes.

title: Honor every messenger, and your reward is coming.
subtitle: Believing in all of Allah's messengers without division
then: Ibn Kathir says this describes the community of Muhammad ﷺ, who {idea}believe in every Book Allah revealed and every prophet He sent.{/idea} He links it to the verse: the Messenger believes in what was revealed to him, and so do the believers. {reward}Allah forgives their sins, if they have any.{/reward}
now: You know a lot about the Prophet ﷺ, but ask yourself what you know about Musa, Ibrahim, Yusuf, or Isa. {trap}They can feel like names from someone else's story.{/trap} The verse says honoring {idea}all of them{/idea} is part of your faith.
old: The earlier prophets are history, not really part of my faith.
new: Every messenger Allah sent is part of the faith I hold.
try: Read the story of one prophet in the Quran this week that you know least about.

title: More proof will not fix a heart that has already said no.
subtitle: Demanding signs after seeing signs
then: People of the Scripture in Madinah asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring down a book from the sky. The verse recalls that Musa's people had {trap}asked for more, to see Allah openly{/trap}, and then worshipped the calf after witnessing miracles in Egypt. Ibn Kathir notes Quraysh made similar demands. {reward}Even so, Allah pardoned them.{/reward}
now: You say you will start praying once you feel certain, once Allah gives you a sign. {trap}But you have had signs.{/trap} The recovery. The near miss. The answered dua. The verse asks whether the problem is {idea}proof, or willingness.{/idea}
old: If Allah showed me one clear sign, I would commit fully.
new: I have already been shown enough. What is missing is my yes.
try: Write down three signs of Allah's care in your own life this year.

title: A mountain over their heads, and a solemn promise taken.
subtitle: How seriously Allah took the covenant
then: Ibn Kathir explains that when Musa's people {trap}refused the rulings of the Tawrah{/trap}, Allah raised the mountain above them and they prostrated. They were told to enter the gate humbly and to honor the Sabbath. Allah took {idea}a firm covenant{/idea} from them. Ibn Kathir notes they later broke it with tricks.
now: You made promises to Allah. In a hospital waiting room. The night before an exam. On the last night of Ramadan. {trap}Once the danger passed, the promise faded.{/trap} The verse reminds you {idea}a promise to Allah is heavy.{/idea}
old: Promises I made to Allah in a hard moment do not really count.
new: A promise to Allah is a covenant, and I want to keep mine.
try: Remember one promise you made to Allah in a hard time. Keep a small part of it today.

title: Our hearts are wrapped, they said. The wrapping was their own doing.
subtitle: Calling a closed heart an excuse
then: The verse lists what some of the Children of Israel did in the past: broke their covenant, rejected signs, killed prophets. They also said {trap}our hearts are wrapped{/trap}, as if that excused them. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah answered: {idea}the seal came because of their disbelief{/idea}, as their hearts grew used to it.
now: You say you are just not a spiritual person. The Quran does not move you. {trap}It sounds like a fact about you.{/trap} But think about what you feed your heart all week. The verse suggests {idea}a heart grows closed by habit{/idea}, and can open the same way.
old: My heart just does not feel faith, so it is not my fault.
new: My habits shape my heart, and I can start reshaping it today.
try: Replace ten minutes of scrolling today with ten minutes of listening to the Quran.

title: Maryam was slandered, and Allah Himself answered for her.
subtitle: A great lie told about a pure woman
then: Ibn Abbas and others explained that some opponents of Isa {trap}accused Maryam of immorality{/trap} and called her son illegitimate. The verse names this {trap}a great slander{/trap} and lists it beside disbelief. The Quran itself {idea}defends Maryam's honor.{/idea}
now: Someone in the family WhatsApp forwards a rumor about a young woman at the mosque. Nobody checks. Everyone adds a comment. {trap}A reputation is destroyed by Thursday.{/trap} The verse shows how seriously Allah takes {idea}a lie against someone's honor.{/idea}
old: Repeating what I heard is harmless if I did not make it up.
new: Passing on a lie about someone's honor is a great wrong in Allah's sight.
try: Next time you hear a rumor about someone's honor, do not pass it on. Defend them.

title: They boasted they killed him. They did not, for certain.
subtitle: A loud claim built on guesswork
then: The verse answers a boast made about Isa son of Maryam. Ibn Kathir explains it was said {trap}in mockery{/trap}, and that another was made to look like him. Those who differ over it {trap}follow only assumption.{/trap} The verse is firm: {idea}they did not kill him, for certain.{/idea}
now: You read a confident headline and share it within seconds. Later it turns out to be wrong. {trap}Loud is not the same as true.{/trap} The verse draws a line between {idea}knowledge and assumption{/idea}, and asks you which one you are speaking from.
old: If people say something confidently enough, it is probably true.
new: Confidence is not knowledge, and I check before I speak.
try: Before you share one piece of news today, check where it came from.

title: When they closed in, Allah raised him to Himself.
subtitle: The Mighty protects those who turn to Him
then: Ibn Kathir narrates that Isa's enemies {trap}surrounded the house{/trap} where he was with his companions. Allah raised him up to Himself. He explains the closing names: Allah is {idea}Mighty, never weak{/idea}, and those who seek refuge in Him {reward}are never left in disgrace{/reward}; and He is Wise in all He decides.
now: You feel cornered. The debt collector calls. The court date is set. Someone at work is clearly trying to push you out. {trap}It looks like they have already won.{/trap} The verse reminds you that {idea}the outcome is with the Mighty{/idea}, not with whoever surrounds you.
old: When I am cornered, there is no way out.
new: Allah can lift me out of any corner, in ways I cannot picture.
try: In your next sujood, ask Allah by name, Al-Aziz, for a way out of what corners you.

title: Every one will believe in him before his death.
subtitle: Isa's return and his testimony on the Day
then: Ibn Abbas explained before his death as {idea}before the death of Isa{/idea}. Ibn Kathir gathers hadiths that Isa will return before the Hour, and then everyone of the People of the Scripture will believe in him. On the Day of Resurrection {reward}he will be a witness{/reward} over them.
now: You argue about faith online and feel you must win every point today. {trap}As if truth depends on your reply.{/trap} The verse shows that Allah will make the truth plain in His own time. {idea}Your job is to live it well{/idea}, not to force the ending.
old: If I do not win this argument, the truth loses.
new: Allah will make the truth clear. I just need to live by it.
try: Step back from one heated religious argument today and spend the energy on a good deed.

title: Wrongdoing can cost you good things you were once allowed.
subtitle: How sins narrow life
then: The verse speaks of the Children of Israel in the past. Ibn Kathir explains that because of {trap}injustice and major sins{/trap}, some good foods that were once lawful became forbidden for them. He also notes they {trap}held themselves and many others back from the truth.{/trap}
now: You cut corners at work, and now your manager double-checks everything you do. You lied once to your parents, and now they ask for proof. {trap}A wrong done quietly can close doors that were open.{/trap} The verse points to {idea}a link between conduct and blessing.{/idea}
old: My private wrongs do not change anything around me.
new: Wrongdoing narrows my life in ways I may not even notice.
try: Think of one blessing that has felt thinner lately. Ask Allah's forgiveness for one specific wrong.

title: Clever tricks do not make taking people's money right.
subtitle: Getting around a prohibition is still disobedience
then: The verse continues describing wrongs from the past. Ibn Kathir says they {trap}had been forbidden riba, yet took it using tricks, ploys and cons{/trap}, and so consumed people's property unjustly. The point is {idea}the trickery itself{/idea}: finding a way around what Allah forbade.
now: The hidden fee buried in the small print. The invoice padded because the client will not check. The deal technically within the rules but meant to squeeze someone. {trap}Clever, and not clean.{/trap} The verse asks: {idea}whose money did I actually take?{/idea}
old: If it is technically within the rules, it is fine.
new: Allah judges what I meant, not just the loophole I used.
try: Look at one way you earn or charge money and ask: would I be comfortable if they saw everything?

title: Deep knowledge leads to faith, prayer, and giving.
subtitle: Those firm in knowledge who recognised the truth
then: After the long list of wrongs, the verse turns. {idea}Not everyone was the same.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said it was revealed about Abdullah bin Salam and others from the People of the Scripture who {reward}embraced Islam{/reward}. Their knowledge was deep enough to recognize the truth.
now: You know a lot. Hadith references, debates, scholars' names. {trap}But knowing is not the same as bowing.{/trap} The verse praises knowledge that ends in {idea}prayer, charity, and certainty{/idea} about the Day. That is how you tell if it is rooted.
old: Knowing a lot about religion means I am close to Allah.
new: Knowledge is rooted when it shows up in my prayer and my giving.
try: Take one thing you learned about the deen this month and act on it today.

title: The same revelation that reached Nuh and Ibrahim reached you.
subtitle: One long line of prophets, one source
then: Ibn Abbas reported that two men, Sukayn and Adi bin Zayd, told the Prophet ﷺ that {trap}they knew of nothing Allah sent down to any human after Musa.{/trap} This verse was the reply. It names prophet after prophet and places Muhammad ﷺ {idea}in the same line of revelation.{/idea}
now: You open the Quran on your phone between meetings. It can feel like just another app. {idea}But the words on that screen come from the same source that spoke to Nuh, Ibrahim and Dawud.{/idea} {reward}You are holding the latest link in a very old chain.{/reward}
old: The Quran is a book I read sometimes.
new: The Quran is the same revelation that reached every prophet, now reaching me.
try: Before reading the Quran today, pause and remember who else received revelation from this same Lord.

title: Some messengers you know by name. Many more you never will.
subtitle: Messengers told and untold, and Musa spoken to directly
then: Ibn Kathir lists about {idea}twenty five prophets named in the Quran{/idea}, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ. The verse adds that there are {idea}others Allah did not tell us about.{/idea} Musa is singled out with a special honor: {reward}Allah spoke to him directly{/reward}, which is why he is called the Kalim.
now: You meet a stranger on a train who is quietly kind to everyone. Nobody will ever write their story. The verse is a reminder that {idea}Allah's work reaches far beyond the stories you know.{/idea} {reward}Untold does not mean unseen.{/reward}
old: If I have not heard of it, it probably did not matter much.
new: Allah's care for people goes far beyond the stories that reached me.
try: Learn the names of three prophets from the Quran you could not name before.

title: Good news and warnings, so no one can say: nobody told me.
subtitle: Why Allah sent messengers at all
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah sent books and messengers to make plain {idea}what He loves and what He dislikes{/idea}, so no one has an argument against Him. The Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}no one loves to give excuse more than Allah{/reward}, and that is why He sent prophets with good news and warnings.
now: A good manager explains the rules on day one, so nobody is blindsided later. Allah did far more than that. {reward}He sent person after person to explain it kindly.{/reward} The verse asks you to notice how much {idea}you have already been told.{/idea}
old: Nobody ever really explained to me what Allah wants.
new: Allah went out of His way to explain, because He loves to give people a chance.
try: Read one short passage of the Quran today as if it were written to you personally.

title: When people deny it, Allah Himself is witness to the Quran.
subtitle: The testimony that does not depend on anyone's approval
then: After listing the prophets, the verse answers those who denied the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}even if they deny and defy you, Allah testifies{/idea} that He sent you the Quran. He sent it {reward}with His knowledge{/reward}, which no messenger or angel could know without His leave.
now: Your coworker rolls their eyes when you step out to pray. A cousin calls your faith old-fashioned. {trap}It stings, and you start doubting yourself.{/trap} The verse steadies you. {idea}The Quran's truth was never waiting for their approval.{/idea}
old: If people around me doubt my faith, maybe I should doubt it too.
new: Allah's witness is enough. Other people's doubt does not change the truth.
try: Next time someone mocks your faith, quietly say: Allah is enough as a witness.

title: Losing your way is one thing. Blocking others is further still.
subtitle: Rejecting the truth and stopping others from it
then: Ibn Kathir explains that these people not only {trap}refused to follow the truth{/trap} themselves, they {trap}worked hard to stop others{/trap} from embracing it. That is why they have strayed so far. The verse looks at {idea}what we do to other people's path{/idea}, not only our own.
now: You tease your younger brother for starting to pray. You tell a friend fasting is pointless. {trap}You think it is just a joke.{/trap} The verse asks you to notice that {idea}your words can push someone away from Allah{/idea}, or toward Him.
old: My attitude to religion only affects me.
new: My words can open or close the way to Allah for someone else.
try: Encourage one person today in a good step they are taking toward Allah.

title: Disbelief joined with wrongdoing closes the road to forgiveness.
subtitle: When rejection and injustice go together
then: Ibn Kathir describes these as people who {trap}reject Allah's signs, His Book and His Messenger{/trap}, wrong themselves and hinder others, and break His limits. The verse describes {idea}the end of that road if it is never left.{/idea} Earlier in this surah, the door of repentance stays open to the living.
now: This verse is sober on purpose. It is not for labeling people. It is for checking your own direction. {trap}Each injustice you excuse makes the next one easier.{/trap} {idea}Turning back today is still possible{/idea}, and that is the mercy hidden in the warning.
old: Warnings like this are about other people.
new: Warnings are road signs for me, telling me where a path ends while I can still turn.
try: Name one wrong you keep excusing in yourself. Ask Allah's forgiveness for it tonight.

title: Only one road is left for them, and it leads to Hell.
subtitle: The road you keep choosing is the road you get
then: The verse completes the one before it. Ibn Kathir explains that the only {trap}path left to those who persist{/trap} in disbelief and injustice is the path of Hell. {idea}And that is easy for Allah{/idea}: no one escapes His judgment by power or cleverness.
now: You do not end up somewhere by accident. You end up there by small turns, made every day. {trap}One skipped prayer, one more lie, one more cruel word.{/trap} The verse asks you to {idea}look at the road you are walking{/idea} and choose its direction now.
old: Where I end up will be decided some other day.
new: Where I end up is being decided by the small turns I make today.
try: Make one small turn toward Allah today that you would want to keep making.

title: The truth has come to you. Believing is better for you.
subtitle: An invitation to all of humanity
then: After stern warnings, the verse turns to {idea}all of humanity{/idea} with an open invitation. Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet ﷺ came with guidance and clear proof, so {reward}following him is better for you.{/reward} If anyone refuses, Allah is far too rich to be harmed by it.
now: A doctor tells you to change your diet, then says: it is for you, not me. {idea}The invitation to faith is like that.{/idea} Allah loses nothing if you ignore it. {reward}You are the one who gains{/reward} if you say yes.
old: Faith is something I do for Allah.
new: Faith is a gift offered to me, for my own good.
try: Thank Allah today, in your own words, for the guidance that reached you.

title: Love a prophet, but never raise him above his rank.
subtitle: The danger of excess in religion
then: The verse calls the People of the Scripture away from {trap}excess in religion{/trap} and to say only the truth about Allah. Ibn Kathir explains Isa as a servant created by the word Be. The Prophet ﷺ warned his own followers too: {idea}do not overpraise me. I am only a servant, so say: Allah's servant and His Messenger.{/idea}
now: You hear people speak of a favorite shaykh as if he could never be wrong. Someone says a saint answers prayers. {trap}Love quietly turns into excess.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ himself warned against it. {idea}Honor people for what Allah gave them, and no more.{/idea}
old: The more I praise someone righteous, the better.
new: Real love for the righteous keeps them as servants of Allah, never more.
try: Next time you praise a scholar or pious person, add: and Allah knows best.

title: The Messiah and the closest angels are never too proud to serve.
subtitle: Worship is an honor, not a humiliation
then: Right after saying who Isa is, the verse says the Messiah {idea}would never disdain being Allah's servant{/idea}, nor would the angels nearest to Him. Ibn Abbas explained the word proud as insolent. Those who are {trap}too proud to worship{/trap} will all be gathered before Him.
now: You feel awkward praying at work. Your friends think kneeling in public is embarrassing. {trap}Pride whispers that bowing makes you small.{/trap} The verse puts you in the best company: {reward}the Messiah and the angels closest to Allah do the very same thing.{/reward}
old: Bowing in worship is a bit humbling and awkward.
new: Bowing to Allah puts me in the company of the Messiah and the angels.
try: Pray one prayer today somewhere you usually feel shy to, calmly and without rushing.

title: Full reward, and then more from His bounty.
subtitle: Two outcomes on the Day of gathering
then: Ibn Kathir explains that after gathering everyone, Allah will judge with justice that is never wrong. The believers who did good will get {reward}their full reward and more{/reward}, from His kindness and ample mercy. Those who {trap}refused to worship out of arrogance{/trap} will find no protector besides Him.
now: You worry that your good deeds are too small to count. The rushed prayers, the little charity, the half-read Quran. {reward}Allah does not just pay what is owed. He adds extra.{/reward} The verse invites you to {idea}offer what you can{/idea}, and trust His generosity with the rest.
old: My good deeds are too small to earn anything real.
new: Allah gives in full and then adds more, so nothing sincere is too small.
try: Do one good deed today and ask Allah to accept it and multiply it.

title: A clear proof and a clear light have been sent to you.
subtitle: The Quran as light for the way
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah tells all people that {idea}a plain, unequivocal proof{/idea} has come from Him, removing every excuse and doubt. Ibn Jurayj and others said the {reward}clear light is the Quran{/reward}, which points to the truth.
now: Your power goes out at night and you fumble for the torch on your phone. Suddenly the stairs, the door, the next step are clear. {reward}The Quran is that light.{/reward} But {trap}it only helps if you switch it on and walk by it.{/trap}
old: The Quran is a holy book to respect from a distance.
new: The Quran is a light for the next step in my actual day.
try: Read one verse this morning and look for a way to walk by it before night.

title: Hold fast to Allah, and He will guide you to Himself.
subtitle: Mercy, bounty, and a straight path
then: Ibn Kathir explains holding fast as {idea}worshipping Allah and relying on Him for every single thing.{/idea} Ibn Jurayj said it means holding fast to the Quran. Such people are admitted to {reward}His mercy and grace{/reward}, and guided on a straight path in this life and the next.
now: Life keeps shaking you. A layoff. A breakup. A diagnosis. {trap}You grab at whatever is nearest.{/trap} The verse offers {idea}one rope that does not snap.{/idea} Hold on to Allah and His Book, and the path leads straight to Him.
old: When life shakes me, I grab whatever is closest.
new: When life shakes me, I hold on to Allah, and He leads me to Himself.
try: In your next hard moment today, before reacting, say: O Allah, I hold on to You.

title: Allah makes it clear so you do not go astray.
subtitle: A closing verse about family and inheritance
then: Al-Bara said this was {idea}among the last verses revealed.{/idea} People asked the Prophet ﷺ about someone who dies leaving no child or parent. Umar said he asked about it more than anything, until the Prophet ﷺ told him {reward}the summer verse at the end of An-Nisa is enough for you.{/reward}
now: Your uncle passes away with no children. Within a week, the family group chat is tense over the house. {trap}Old grudges come out over money.{/trap} The surah that began with caring for orphans and family ends here: {idea}Allah made it clear so you would not go astray.{/idea}
old: Inheritance is just paperwork and whoever is quickest.
new: How I handle a family's wealth after death is part of my faith.
try: If an inheritance ever touches your family, ask a qualified scholar early, before tempers rise.
